predict.question: This vinegar titration's equivalence point sits at pH 8.6, not 7. Which indicator marks it — phenolphthalein (turns 8.2–10) or methyl orange (turns 3.1–4.4)?
options: Either — an indicator is a colour signal, and any colour signal will do
Phenolphthalein: its turn sits on the endpoint. Methyl orange fires long before, deep in the buffer region
Methyl orange — orange is easier to see against white than pale pink
predict.misconception: An indicator is not a bell that rings at 'done' — it is a weak acid that changes form at its own pKa, wherever that is. The choice is an alignment problem: the indicator's transition window must sit on the titration's pH jump. Phenolphthalein's window straddles this endpoint's 8.6; methyl orange's window was crossed back near pH 4, in the slow buffer climb, where its colour change marks nothing of analytical interest at all.

diagnosis.reveals: All indicators are interchangeable signals: the chemistry of the dye plays no role, so any colour change means 'stop'.
diagnosis.next: Run the half-titrated flask (v2): methyl orange already reads orange at pH 4.69, half the base still unspent. An analyst stopping at that signal would report half the true concentration — the wrong indicator does not merely inconvenience, it answers a different question.

diagnosis.reveals: The indicator is chosen for visibility — an aesthetic decision about colours, with the pH axis absent from the choice entirely.
diagnosis.next: Visibility is real but secondary: the question an indicator answers is WHERE it turns, not how prettily. `weak-acid-endpoint-is-alkaline` computed this endpoint at 8.8-adjacent rather than 7 — that number is the whole reason phenolphthalein is the standard choice for weak-acid titrations, and it looked arbitrary only until the endpoint was computed.

registers.lv1: Two magic dyes. One stays invisible until the very moment the sour is used up — then the flask blushes pink. The other changed colour ages ago, while there was still plenty of sour left. Only one of them is telling you when to stop.
registers.lv2: An indicator is a weak acid with differently coloured forms; it turns near its own pKa. Phenolphthalein (transition ≈8.2–10) straddles this titration's equivalence point — the bench reads pH 8.62 and renders the flask pink. Methyl orange (≈3.1–4.4) completed its change inside the buffer region: v2, only half-titrated, already shows orange at pH 4.69.
registers.lv3: The colours are computed, not curated per pH: each indicator carries two measured spectra (acid and base form), the engine populates the forms by the Henderson–Hasselbalch ratio at the solved pH, and Beer–Lambert over the CIE observer renders the mixture — the pink at 8.62 and the orange at 4.69 are the same arithmetic that makes permanganate purple. One dosing honesty: the bench doses pure substance, so the micromole amounts here play the role of the real lab's 'two drops of indicator solution' — drop-based doses of the pure dye would be a hundredfold overdose and saturate every hue toward black.

setup.script:
add v1 water 100mL
add v1 NaCl 0.001mol
add v1 bromothymol_blue 0.000002mol
add v1 HCl 0.0005mol
add v1 NaOH 0.001mol

predict.question: Bromothymol blue is yellow in acid and blue in base. Near pH 7, what colour is the solution?
options: Yellow or blue, whichever it has flipped to — an indicator is a switch
Green — both forms are present at once, and their colours mix
Colourless — halfway between, the two colours cancel out
predict.misconception: An indicator is not a switch but an equilibrium: at pH near its pKa, roughly half the molecules are in each form, simultaneously. Half the dye absorbing like the yellow form plus half absorbing like the blue form transmits green — the same way mixing paints does, because absorbances add. Cancellation is how opposing *lights* behave; absorbing dyes only ever subtract more.

diagnosis.reveals: The indicator as a binary switch: each molecule — or the whole beaker — is in exactly one state, and 'transition range' just means uncertainty about which.
diagnosis.next: Walk the beaker through all three colours in this entry's script: yellow in acid, blue-green near neutral, blue in base. A switch has no stable middle; an equilibrium population does, and the green IS the population statement — you are seeing the ratio.

diagnosis.reveals: Colours as opposites that annul: yellow plus blue equals nothing, the way positive and negative do.
diagnosis.next: Sort out lights from dyes: complementary LIGHTS can cancel to white, but a dye works by absorbing, and two absorbers in one beaker absorb the union — red taken by one form, orange-red by the other, leaving green to pass. Absorbances add; they never subtract. The bench's colour engine literally adds the two spectra before rendering.

registers.lv1: This dye is yellow in sour water and blue in soapy water. In plain water it is green — because it is half yellow-form and half blue-form at the same time, and your eye adds them up.
registers.lv2: The indicator equilibrium HInd ⇌ H⁺ + Ind⁻ sits at its pKa near 7: in acid the yellow HInd dominates, in base the blue Ind⁻, and near neutral both are populated — the bench renders yellow, then blue-green, then blue as this script swings the same beaker across the scale.
registers.lv3: The green never exists as a curated colour anywhere in the data: the engine holds one measured spectrum per form, populates the forms by the computed ratio at the solved pH, sums the absorbances, and integrates over the CIE 1931 observer. The mid-colour is therefore a *prediction* that mixing works — the same additivity claim the README makes for permanganate's concentration-dependent hue, here testable by eye at every pH in between. Endpoint honesty: the script parks the beaker at pH 11.63 (fully blue) so the pH claim is checkable; the blue-green reading occurs mid-script, at the near-neutral stop.

setup.script:
add v1 water 1000mL
add v1 NaCl 5.844g
measure v1 balance

predict.question: You weigh out 5.844 g of table salt. The bench asks how many moles that is. Sodium chloride's molar mass is 58.443 g/mol. What does the engine report going in?
options: 5.844 mol — the number you weighed
58.443 mol — the molar mass
It depends how much water you put it in
predict.misconception: The last option is the common one: learners expect the amount of substance to change when the solution is diluted. It does not — n is a property of the sample you weighed, and only concentration depends on the volume. The first is the rawer error of using grams as if they were moles.

diagnosis.reveals: Grams and moles are two names for one 'amount', converting by relabelling — the balance said 5.844, so 5.844 it is, in whatever unit the question wants.
diagnosis.next: Weigh out 58.443 g instead and ask again: one mole, exactly. A mole is a count, priced in grams by the molar mass — the balance reads the price, never the count.

diagnosis.reveals: The molar mass is read as the answer: the biggest, most official-looking number on the page must be the quantity asked for, and the division's direction is lost.
diagnosis.next: Sanity-check by size before dividing either way: 58 mol of salt would be three and a half kilograms, and the balance is holding six grams. When a formula's direction is uncertain, the absurd magnitude is the tell.

diagnosis.reveals: Amount and concentration are welded: dilute it and there is 'less salt', so n must shrink with the water it sits in.
diagnosis.next: Run `concentration-is-a-ratio`: the same 5.844 g into 100 mL and into 200 mL, and both vessels `inspect` to 0.1000 mol. Only the mol-per-litre moved — the count you weighed is not negotiable by water.

registers.lv1: Weighing tells you how heavy something is. Counting tells you how many pieces there are. Chemistry needs the count, because reactions pair pieces up — and the balance is how you get to the count, since every substance has a fixed weight per piece.
registers.lv2: n = m / M. 5.844 g ÷ 58.443 g/mol = 0.1000 mol, and the bench confirms 0.1000 mol going in. In 1.000 L that is a 0.1 mol/L solution; the total mass on the balance, 1002.84 g, is the litre of water plus the salt, because nothing left.
registers.lv3: The registry carries M = 58.443 g/mol from the IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights, so the conversion is exact to the data's own precision rather than to a rounded 58.5. The 0.1000 mol then enters PHREEQC as a total-element constraint, and the pH of 6.98 rather than 7.00 is the ionic-strength correction on the water's own autoprotolysis, not an artefact.

predict.question: The same 5.844 g of salt goes into 100 mL in one beaker and 200 mL in another. Which beaker holds more sodium chloride?
options: The 100 mL beaker — it is more concentrated
The 200 mL beaker — there is more liquid
Neither: both hold 0.1000 mol; only the concentration differs
predict.misconception: Concentration and amount get welded together. A strong cup of tea does not contain more tea than a weak bucket of it. The engine separates the two explicitly: both vessels report 0.1000 mol of chloride, and the ionic strengths differ by exactly a factor of two.

diagnosis.reveals: 'More concentrated' is read as 'containing more' — intensity mistaken for quantity, the strong cup of tea holding more tea than the weak bucket.
diagnosis.next: Evaporate both to dryness: identical crystals, 5.84 g each, back on the same balance. Two solutions that differ in everything the tongue would notice return the same salt, because the salt never differed.

diagnosis.reveals: Solute scales with solution: more liquid must hold more stuff, as if the water manufactured salt to fill itself.
diagnosis.next: Follow the salt's paper trail: it entered once, on the balance, before any water was chosen. `measure` both vessels — they differ by exactly the extra water's mass, and by nothing else.

registers.lv1: Two beakers, the same spoonful of salt, different amounts of water. The small one tastes saltier — but there is not more salt in it. 'How much' and 'how strong' are two different questions, and mixing them up is one of the easiest mistakes to make.
registers.lv2: c = n / V. 0.1000 mol in 0.100 L is 1.00 mol/L; in 0.200 L it is 0.50 mol/L. The bench reports the ionic strength of the two solutions as 1.0030 m and 0.5015 m — exactly the halving, because for a 1:1 salt like NaCl the ionic strength equals the molality.
registers.lv3: Ionic strength I = ½ Σ cᵢ zᵢ², which for a 1:1 electrolyte collapses to the concentration itself; that identity is why the two numbers look like the concentrations. The small excess over 1.0000 (1.0030 m) is molality against molarity: the litre of solution is not a litre of water, and PHREEQC works in mol per kg of water throughout.

measure v1 ph

predict.question: An acid reads pH 2.04. You add nine times as much water again, so the volume is ten times what it was. What does the meter read now?
options: pH 3.0 — a tenfold dilution costs one pH unit
pH 7.0 — water is neutral, so diluting makes it neutral
pH 20.4 — ten times the pH
pH 2.04 — the acid is still in there
predict.misconception: Two errors are common and both are about the logarithm. 'Ten times the volume, ten times the pH' treats pH as if it were the concentration; and 'dilution neutralises' forgets that no amount of water reaches pH 7 — you approach it and never arrive, because the acid is still all there.

diagnosis.reveals: Mixing averages the labels: water 'is pH 7', so enough of it drags the mixture to 7 the way white paint lightens red — neutrality as an ingredient rather than an absence.
diagnosis.next: Keep diluting, tenfold at a time, and read the meter each round: 3, then 4, then 5 — one unit per decade, creeping toward 7 and never arriving, because every proton that came in is still in there.

diagnosis.reveals: pH is proportional to 'how much': the logarithm is absent, so ten times the volume multiplies the reading by ten.
diagnosis.next: Notice what 20.4 would even mean: the scale counts powers of ten of hydrogen-ion activity, which is why water's whole world fits between about 0 and 14. A tenfold change moves it by exactly one — to 3.0, as the meter shows.

diagnosis.reveals: pH travels with the acid like a colour: as long as the acid exists, its label persists — crowding plays no role in the reading.
diagnosis.next: Run it and hold both facts at once: `inspect` shows the same moles of acid, and the meter moves anyway. pH belongs to the solution, not to the substance — it prices how crowded the protons are, not whether they exist.

registers.lv1: Add water to an acid and it gets weaker — but it never turns into water. The acid you put in is still there; it just has more room. On the meter the number climbs, and it climbs by one step for every tenfold splash of water, not by ten.
registers.lv2: c₁V₁ = c₂V₂. 0.001 mol in 100 mL is 0.01 mol/L; the meter reads pH 2.04. Take the volume to 1.000 L and the concentration is 0.001 mol/L — the meter reads pH 3.01. One pH unit per factor of ten, because pH is a logarithm.
registers.lv3: The moles of H⁺ are conserved exactly across the dilution; what changes is the activity, and with it the measured pH. Note the reading is 2.04 rather than 2.00 and 3.01 rather than 3.00: at I ≈ 0.01 m the activity coefficient is ≈0.90, and PHREEQC reports pH as −log a(H⁺), not −log c(H⁺). Textbooks assume γ = 1 and quietly lose that hundredth.

measure v1 balance

predict.question: Burn 2.40 g of magnesium ribbon completely. The balanced equation is 2 Mg + O₂ → 2 MgO. M(Mg) = 24.305, M(MgO) = 40.304 g/mol. What mass of white powder is left?
options: 2.40 g — mass is conserved
1.44 g — some burns away
4.80 g — one oxygen per magnesium doubles it
predict.misconception: The first option is conservation of mass misapplied: mass is conserved in the universe, not in an open crucible that is drawing oxygen out of the room. The last comes from reading '2 Mg + O₂' as though each magnesium takes a whole O₂ rather than half of one.

diagnosis.reveals: Conservation applied to the crucible instead of the system: what the balance saw at the start is all there is, and the invisible reactant drawn from the room has no line in the ledger.
diagnosis.next: `burning-makes-it-heavier` is this confrontation staged on a balance: the ash outweighs the ribbon by precisely the oxygen's mass. Conservation holds — over ribbon plus air, not over the crucible alone.

diagnosis.reveals: Burning is loss: fire consumes, so less remains — the campfire's log-to-ash prototype applied to a metal.
diagnosis.next: Weigh it: 3.98 g from 2.40. The campfire was not lying — its loss left as gas. Magnesium's product is a solid, so the oxygen it took stays on the balance (`burning-makes-it-lighter` runs the prototype itself, for contrast).

diagnosis.reveals: The coefficients read pairwise: '2 Mg + O₂' as each magnesium taking a whole O₂, the 2:1 ratio collapsed into 1:1.
diagnosis.next: Count atoms through the equation: two magnesiums share one O₂ — one oxygen atom each, 16 g per mole of metal, not 32. The molar masses in the question already contain the answer: 2.40 g × 40.304/24.305 = 3.98 g.

registers.lv1: Weigh the ribbon: 2.40 g. Burn it. Weigh the ash: 3.98 g. Do it again with twice as much ribbon and you get twice as much ash — the relationship between what you start with and what you end with is fixed, and once you know it for one piece you know it for every piece.
registers.lv2: 0.0987 mol of Mg (2.40 g ÷ 24.305 g/mol) gives 0.0987 mol of MgO by the 2:2 ratio in the equation, which is 3.98 g (× 40.304 g/mol). The bench reports exactly 0.0987 mol of MgO and a balance reading of 3.98 g. The equation is not decoration — it is the conversion factor.
registers.lv3: The 1:1 mole ratio survives because the Gibbs minimiser conserves the magnesium element budget exactly; oxygen is drawn from the atmospheric reservoir rather than the vessel's inventory, which is what makes the mass ratio 40.304/24.305 = 1.658 appear on the balance. At the 3042 K the solve settles to, gaseous Mg and MgO are thermodynamically accessible; they do not appear in the products because the condensed oxide dominates at 1 bar.

predict.question: Beaker 1: 0.0100 mol of chloride and 0.0200 mol of silver. Beaker 2: 0.0200 mol of chloride and 0.0100 mol of silver. Which makes more silver chloride?
options: Beaker 1 — it has more silver, and silver is the heavy part
Beaker 2 — it has more chloride
Neither: both make 0.0100 mol, set by whichever ion runs out first
predict.misconception: Learners reliably add the reagents up rather than pairing them off. The reaction is one silver to one chloride: the partner in short supply decides the answer and the surplus simply sits there. Both beakers hold 0.0300 mol of reactant in total and both give exactly 0.0100 mol of precipitate.

diagnosis.reveals: The yield follows the 'important' reagent: silver is the heavy, expensive, name-giving part, so more silver means more silver chloride — pairing-off is not in the picture.
diagnosis.next: Run both and filter: two identical 0.0100 mol cakes. Then `inspect` what remains dissolved — beaker 1 still holds its extra silver, doing nothing. Importance is not a stoichiometric quantity.

diagnosis.reveals: The mirror of the same error: more of either ingredient means more product — amounts add, rather than pair.
diagnosis.next: Pair them off like dance partners: each AgCl needs exactly one of each ion, so the shorter queue ends the dance — at 0.0100 mol in both rooms. The totals being equal (0.0300 mol each) is the trap the question sets.

registers.lv1: Two beakers get the same total amount of chemical, just split differently — one has extra silver, the other extra salt. Both go cloudy, and both produce exactly the same amount of white solid. Whatever runs out first is what stops the reaction; the leftovers do nothing but stay dissolved.
registers.lv2: Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl↓ is a 1:1 reaction. Beaker 1: 0.0100 mol Cl⁻ is limiting against 0.0200 mol Ag⁺. Beaker 2: 0.0100 mol Ag⁺ is limiting against 0.0200 mol Cl⁻. The bench reports 0.0100 mol of AgCl in both. Work out the moles of each, take the smaller, and you have predicted the answer before running it.
registers.lv3: The solver does not apply a limiting-reagent rule — it minimises free energy subject to element balances, and the 1:1 stoichiometry falls out of the mass-action constraint on Ksp(AgCl) ≈ 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰. The two beakers differ in what remains dissolved: excess Ag⁺ suppresses residual chloride and vice versa, the common-ion effect, and the final pH differs slightly (6.90 against 7.07) because nitrate and chloride do not affect the proton balance identically.

predict.question: 0.0100 mol of each reagent, filtered and dried. The theoretical yield is 1.43 g. A class of thirty does this and reports yields between 71% and 96%. Where did the missing silver chloride go?
options: The reaction did not finish — some silver stayed as Ag⁺
Mostly onto the filter paper, the beaker wall and the wash water
It decomposed while drying
predict.misconception: A yield under 100% gets read as a statement about the chemistry, so learners go looking for an incomplete reaction. Here it is almost entirely mechanical loss. The engine makes that visible by reporting 1.43 g — the full theoretical yield — because it models the chemistry and nothing else: no filter paper, no splashes, no scraping. The residual dissolved silver is real but tiny, around 10⁻⁶ mol.

diagnosis.reveals: Every shortfall is chemistry's fault: a yield under 100% means the reaction stopped early, because the apparatus is invisible in the account.
diagnosis.next: Compare the two worlds: this bench models chemistry with no filter paper, no beaker walls, no splashes — and reports the full 1.43 g, with the genuinely-unreacted silver near 10⁻⁶ mol, a thousandth of what the class lost. The missing grams are on the equipment, which is why careful gravimetric work weighs the filter paper too.

diagnosis.reveals: A reaction is invented to cover a bookkeeping gap: mass is missing, so a plausible-sounding process nobody observed — decomposition on drying — gets the blame.
diagnosis.next: Look at the loss pattern before blaming chemistry: thirty students scattered from 71% to 96%. A decomposition at a shared drying temperature would take a similar bite from everyone; handling losses scatter exactly like this. The spread is the fingerprint.

registers.lv1: Filter the cloudy mixture and a white paste stays on the paper. Dry it and weigh it. The number you get is almost never the number you calculated — and in a real lab, that gap is mostly stuff stuck to the glass, not chemistry going wrong.
registers.lv2: The limiting reagent gives 0.0100 mol of AgCl, which at 143.32 g/mol is a theoretical yield of 1.43 g. The bench filters and weighs 1.43 g in v1, and the filtrate v2 weighs 499.35 g. Percentage yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100; here it is essentially 100%, so any shortfall in a real experiment is loss, not incomplete reaction.
registers.lv3: The filtrate still holds silver and chloride at the level Ksp demands — the inspect view shows both at the fourth-decimal floor — so the 'complete' precipitation is complete only to within the solubility product, about 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L each in pure water. That residue is a real, calculable loss and is the reason gravimetric analysis washes with dilute nitric acid rather than water. What the engine cannot model is the paper, and it does not pretend to.

predict.question: 4.2 g of baking soda (0.0500 mol) is fizzed with a big excess of vinegar — four times more acid than needed. How much CO₂ comes off?
options: More than with the exact amount, because more acid means more reaction
0.0500 mol — every carbon atom in the gas came from the bicarbonate
0.2000 mol — one per molecule of acid
predict.misconception: Pouring in more acid feels like it should give more fizz, and it does look more violent. But the carbon in the carbon dioxide can only have come from the carbonate, and there are 0.0500 mol of carbon atoms in the beaker. Excess acid changes the rate and the final pH; it cannot change the element budget.

diagnosis.reveals: Reagents are a throttle: more in, more out — and the extra violence of the excess-acid fizz is read as extra yield rather than extra speed.
diagnosis.next: Watch the balance instead of the froth: double the acid, then quadruple it — the mass lost as gas is the same every time, because the carbon count never changed. Violence is a rate; yield is a budget.

diagnosis.reveals: The gas is credited to the acid: carbon dioxide as something the vinegar makes, one per molecule, rather than something released from the carbonate.
diagnosis.next: Trace the atoms: vinegar's own carbons stay in the beaker as acetate — `inspect` shows them still dissolved after the fizz — and the CO₂ count matches the bicarbonate's 0.0500 mol exactly. The gas carries the carbonate's carbon, and only that.

registers.lv1: Baking soda plus vinegar fizzes. Use four times as much vinegar and it fizzes harder and faster — but exactly the same amount of gas comes out in the end. Every bubble is made of atoms that were sitting in the powder; when they have all left, there is nothing more to give.
registers.lv2: 0.0500 mol NaHCO₃ carries 0.0500 mol of carbon. The bench releases 0.0183 mol on dissolving alone (the solution outgasses towards atmospheric pCO₂) and a further 0.0317 mol on acidification — 0.0500 mol exactly. Run it with 0.0599 mol of acid instead of 0.1998 and you get the same 0.0500 mol; only the final pH differs, 5.30 against 4.13.
registers.lv3: Total dissolved inorganic carbon is fixed by the addition; what the acid does is shift the carbonate speciation until the solution supersaturates against log p(CO₂) = −3.408 and the excess exsolves. The split between the two steps is therefore not a stoichiometric fact but a Henry's-law one, and it moves if the atmosphere does. The sum does not move: element budgets are the hardest constraint in the solve.

setup.script:

add v1 NaHCO3 4.2g
measure v1 balance

predict.question: The beaker reads 252.66 g. You add 3.60 g of vinegar and it fizzes. What does the balance read when the fizzing stops?
options: 256.26 g — mass is always conserved
254.84 g — about 1.4 g lighter than expected
252.66 g — the acid is consumed
predict.misconception: 'Mass is conserved' is taught as a law and then applied to a container rather than to a system. It is the atoms that are conserved; they are simply not all in the beaker any more. Stopper the flask and the reading does become 256.26 g — which is why the closed-vessel version of this experiment is the one Lavoisier needed.

diagnosis.reveals: The beaker is the universe: the law says conserved, the balance holds the beaker, so the reading must add up — the possibility of mass leaving through the open top is not in the account.
diagnosis.next: Stopper it: the closed flask reads 256.26 g exactly, and the law is vindicated the moment the boundary is drawn honestly. Lavoisier's sealed vessels existed for precisely this reason — the law was only ever provable with the lid on.

diagnosis.reveals: 'Consumed' means 'gone': used-up reactants vanish, so the added vinegar should leave no trace on the balance at all.
diagnosis.next: Audit the vinegar's atoms: the acetate and the water it became are still in the beaker, weighing what they weigh; only the CO₂'s 1.4 g left. Adding 3.60 g and reading +2.18 g is a subtraction with a story — not a disappearance.

registers.lv1: Put the beaker on the scales and write the number down. Add the vinegar. Watch the number fall as it fizzes. Nothing was destroyed — the bubbles left the beaker and took their weight with them, and if you had put a lid on, the number would not have moved at all.
registers.lv2: 252.66 g + 3.60 g = 256.26 g if nothing leaves. The balance reads 254.84 g, so 1.42 g went missing. The bench reports 0.0317 mol of CO₂ evolved; 0.0317 × 44.009 g/mol = 1.40 g. The missing mass is the gas, to within the accounting.
registers.lv3: The engine's element bookkeeping is exact; the vessel's mass is not conserved because the gas phase is modelled as escaping to the reservoir, exactly as an open beaker does. The small residual between 1.42 g measured and 1.40 g of CO₂ is water leaving with it and the rounding on the reported moles — worth stating rather than smoothing, because in a real experiment the same discrepancy is real and has the same cause.

setup.script:
add v1 water 1000mL
add v1 HCl 0.1mol
measure v1 ph

predict.question: 0.100 mol of hydrochloric acid in a litre of water. The textbook formula pH = −log[H⁺] gives 1.00. What does the meter read?
options: Exactly 1.00
1.08 — a little above, because the meter responds to activity, not concentration
0.92 — a little below
predict.misconception: pH = −log c is taught as a definition when it is an approximation that holds when ions are far apart. At 0.1 mol/L they are not: each proton is surrounded by a cloud of counter-ions that shields it, and the electrode feels the shielded version. The gap is small here and grows with concentration — which is exactly why lv3 exists.

diagnosis.reveals: The formula is the definition, so the meter must obey it — a disagreeing meter is broken, and 'activity' has no slot in the picture.
diagnosis.next: Dilute and watch the gap close: at 0.001 mol/L (`strong-acid`) formula and meter agree to the second decimal; at 0.1 they part by 0.08. A definition's error does not shrink with dilution — an approximation's does, and that behaviour is the diagnosis.

diagnosis.reveals: A correction is expected but its direction is guessed — the crowding is imagined to concentrate the acid's punch rather than damp it, so corrections land by coin-flip.
diagnosis.next: Let the physics fix the sign: every proton drags a cloud of counter-ions that screens it, so the electrode always feels *less* than the count in solutions like this — the reading lands above the naive number, never below. A correction whose sign you can derive is chemistry; one you guess is decoration.

registers.lv1: A pH meter does not count acid particles. It responds to how strongly the acid is pushing, and in a crowded solution the particles get in each other's way, so the push is slightly weaker than the count suggests. The meter tells you what the solution does, which is the number that matters.
registers.lv2: 0.100 mol in 1.000 L is 0.100 mol/L. Complete dissociation gives [H⁺] = 0.100, so −log[H⁺] = 1.00. The meter reads 1.08. The formula is right about the count and slightly wrong about the reading, and the difference is not experimental error — it is reproducible.
registers.lv3: pH is defined as −log a(H⁺), and a = γc. At I = 0.1 m the WATEQ Debye–Hückel extension gives γ(H⁺) ≈ 0.83, so pH = −log(0.83 × 0.100) = 1.08 — which is what PHREEQC computes and reports. Compare the same acid at 0.001 mol/L, where γ ≈ 0.96 and the correction is a hundredth: the approximation is not wrong, it has a validity range, and this is a place where the learner can watch it expire.

new
add v2 water 1000mL

predict.question: Both beakers get 0.100 mol of acid in a litre. One is hydrochloric acid, one is vinegar's acetic acid. The hydrochloric reads pH 1.08. What does the acetic acid read?
options: 1.08 as well — same concentration, same pH
2.88 — about 60 times fewer free protons
4.76 — the pKa
7.00 — vinegar is food, so it must be neutral
predict.misconception: The pH = −log c habit, freshly learned, is applied to the acetic acid and produces 1.00 — the first option. It fails because the formula silently assumed the acid was fully dissociated. Choosing the pKa is the next mistake along: pH equals pKa only in a buffer, where acid and conjugate base are equal, and this beaker has almost no acetate in it.

diagnosis.reveals: pH = −log c with c the label concentration: the formula's hidden assumption — that every molecule has dissociated — has never surfaced, so all acids of one concentration read alike.
diagnosis.next: `inspect` the acetic beaker at lv3: nearly all of the 0.100 mol is still intact CH₃COOH, holding its proton. The meter prices only the free protons, and there are about sixty times fewer of them than the label promised.

diagnosis.reveals: The pKa is the acid's pH — the one number remembered about vinegar, deployed wherever vinegar appears, with the buffer condition that came attached to it lost in transit.
diagnosis.next: Make the condition true and the number becomes right: `half-neutralised-vinegar` neutralises half, [HA] equals [A⁻], and the meter reads the pKa on the nose. This beaker has almost no acetate, so the equality it needs fails by miles.

diagnosis.reveals: Edible means mild means pH 7: the category 'food' is answering a chemistry question, with safety and neutrality fused into one scale.
diagnosis.next: Measure what you already eat: this very beaker is vinegar at 2.88, and you sprinkle it on chips. Edibility is a fact about dose and biology; the meter is measuring something else entirely, and the two scales only look alike until one of them is read.

registers.lv1: Same amount of acid, same amount of water, two very different meter readings. The strong one gives all its acidity up at once; the weak one holds most of it back and only lets a little go. That is why vinegar is safe to eat and hydrochloric acid at the same strength is not.
registers.lv2: The naive calculation, pH = −log(0.100) = 1.00, is right for HCl (to within the activity correction — 1.08) and badly wrong for acetic acid, where the meter reads 2.88. Acetic acid only partly dissociates: pH ≈ ½(pKa − log c) = ½(4.76 + 1.00) = 2.88. You must know the Ka before you can calculate the pH, and that is the whole difference between a strong acid and a weak one.
registers.lv3: PHREEQC does not apply the weak-acid formula either; it solves the mass-action equation H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻ ⇌ CH₃COOH (pKa ≈ 4.76 from minteq.v4.dat) simultaneously with charge and mass balance, and the pH falls out. The agreement with the ½(pKa − log c) shortcut at 2.88 is a check on the shortcut's assumptions — that dissociation is small and water's own protons are negligible — both of which hold here and both of which fail at 10⁻⁵ mol/L.

setup.script:
add v1 water 100mL
add v1 CaCl2 11.098g
measure v1 thermometer

predict.question: 0.1000 mol of calcium chloride (ΔH_dis = −82.8 kJ/mol) dissolves in 100 mL of water. Water's molar heat capacity is 75.3 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹ and 100 mL is 5.53 mol. How warm does it get, starting from 25.0 °C?
options: About 27 °C — a couple of degrees
About 45 °C
About 108 °C — it would boil
It stays at 25 °C; dissolving is a physical change, not a chemical one
predict.misconception: The last option is the deep one: dissolving gets filed under 'physical change' and physical changes are assumed not to involve energy. Breaking an ionic lattice and hydrating the ions are both large energy terms, and their difference is what the thermometer reads. The 108 °C answer comes from dividing by the mass in grams while using a molar heat capacity.

diagnosis.reveals: The energy is conceded but sized by feel: kilojoules sound small, so degrees must be few — the division that would settle it is never actually done.
diagnosis.next: Do the division the question hands you: 8.28 kJ into 5.53 mol × 75.3 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹ is 416 J/K, so +19.9 K. Committing to the arithmetic before the thermometer settles it is the entire exercise.

diagnosis.reveals: Units crossed mid-formula: grams sat under a molar heat capacity, and the resulting large number felt like chemistry happening rather than like an error.
diagnosis.next: Carry the units through: J ÷ (mol × J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹) leaves kelvin; grams under a molar capacity leaves nonsense wearing a temperature's clothes. Units are not decoration — they are the check that catches this before the water conspicuously fails to boil.

diagnosis.reveals: Taxonomy doing physics: 'physical change' is a no-energy category, so classifying the event answers the thermometer's question.
diagnosis.next: The categories do not hold the energy — the lattice and the hydration shells do. Run `cold-from-baking-soda` beside this: the same 'physical change' with the opposite sign. A taxonomy that predicts zero cannot predict both +20 K and −4 K; an energy balance predicts both.

registers.lv1: The cup gets genuinely hot — too hot to hold comfortably — and nothing was burned and nothing was plugged in. Pulling a crystal apart and wrapping water round the pieces releases more energy than it costs, and the surplus has nowhere to go except into the water.
registers.lv2: q = n × ΔH_dis = 0.1000 mol × 82.8 kJ/mol = 8.28 kJ released. The water is 100 mL, 5.5343 mol, at 75.3 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹, so ΔT = 8280 J ÷ 416.7 J/K = 19.9 K. From 25.0 °C that predicts 44.9 °C, and the thermometer reads 44.87 °C. The calculation is not an exercise — it is the reading.
registers.lv3: The heat goes into the water alone: the dissolved Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ carry no modelled heat capacity, since partial molar heat capacities of aqueous ions are small and often negative and are not curated at this stage. That is an approximation with a known sign, and it is why the computed 44.87 °C sits marginally above a full calorimetric treatment. The vessel is adiabatic, so nothing is lost to a cup or to the room — the real experiment always reads lower, and the gap is the calorimeter constant.

predict.question: 0.1000 mol of baking soda goes into 100 mL of water at 25.0 °C. ΔH_dis = +16.7 kJ/mol. What does the thermometer say?
options: Warmer — dissolving always releases energy
21.0 °C — about four degrees colder
Unchanged — the water is what holds the temperature
predict.misconception: Having just watched calcium chloride heat a cup, learners generalise: dissolving warms things. The sign of ΔH_dis is a property of the substance, not of dissolving. Baking soda, potassium chloride and ammonium nitrate all go the other way, and an instant cold pack is exactly this experiment.

diagnosis.reveals: Last experiment's result, promoted to a law: dissolving warms things, because the memorable one did.
diagnosis.next: Run `hot-pack-arithmetic` and this beaker back to back: the sign travels with the substance, not with the operation. ΔH_dis here is +16.7 kJ/mol, and the thermometer obeys the sign, not the habit.

diagnosis.reveals: Water as a thermal anchor: a big steady liquid that a spoonful of powder cannot move — heat capacity mistaken for immunity.
diagnosis.next: Heat capacity is a price, not a veto: withdrawing 1.67 kJ from 416 J/K of water costs 4.0 K, and the thermometer pays it. A large capacity makes moves smaller — `two-vessels-one-variable` prices exactly that — but never zero.

registers.lv1: Same cup, same water, different powder — and this one goes cold instead of hot. That is not a trick or a different kind of stirring; some substances have to borrow energy from the water to come apart, and the water is left colder for lending it.
registers.lv2: q = 0.1000 mol × (+16.7 kJ/mol) = +1.67 kJ absorbed. ΔT = −1670 J ÷ 416.7 J/K = −4.0 K, so 25.0 °C → 21.0 °C, and the thermometer reads 21.02 °C. Potassium chloride at +17.2 kJ/mol gives 20.87 °C in the same cup — nearly the same, because the enthalpies are nearly the same.
registers.lv3: Endothermic dissolution means the lattice enthalpy exceeds the sum of the hydration enthalpies; the deficit comes out of the solution's sensible heat in an adiabatic vessel. Note the bench also reports 0.0424 mol of CO₂ leaving: a bicarbonate solution at pH 10.07 is supersaturated against atmospheric pCO₂ and outgasses. That carbonate chemistry is real and independent of the thermal effect, which is why both events appear.

predict.question: The same 0.1000 mol of calcium chloride goes into 100 mL in one cup and 200 mL in another. The first reaches 44.87 °C. What does the second reach?
options: 44.87 °C — the same energy was released
34.93 °C — the same energy, spread through twice as much water
89.7 °C — twice the water, twice the heating
predict.misconception: The first option confuses energy with temperature — they are not the same quantity, and this pair of cups is the cheapest way to feel the difference. Exactly the same 8.28 kJ is released in both; the thermometer reads the energy per unit of stuff it has to warm, so doubling the water halves the rise.

diagnosis.reveals: Energy and temperature are one quantity: 'the heat' is what the thermometer reads, so the same salt must give the same reading anywhere.
diagnosis.next: Hold both numbers at once: 8.28 kJ released in each cup — identical — and +19.9 K in one against +9.9 K in the other. The thermometer reads energy per amount of stuff to warm; this pair of cups is the cheapest instrument that can tell those two quantities apart.

diagnosis.reveals: More water is read as more reaction: the solvent is promoted to a reagent, so doubling it should double the heat.
diagnosis.next: `inspect` both cups: identical 0.1000 mol dissolved, identical energy released. The water only divides the heat — if it fed the reaction, the salt would somehow have to know how much water was watching it dissolve.

registers.lv1: Change one thing and nothing else. Two cups, the same powder, the same starting temperature — only the amount of water is different. Then whatever the thermometers do differently, you know what caused it. Change two things at once and you have learned nothing, however carefully you measured.
registers.lv2: Identical q = 8.28 kJ in both cups. ΔT = q/(n·Cp): 8280 ÷ 416.7 = 19.9 K in 100 mL, and 8280 ÷ 833.5 = 9.9 K in 200 mL. The bench gives 44.87 °C and 34.93 °C from 25.0 °C — 19.87 K and 9.93 K. The halving is exact because the only thing that changed was the denominator.
registers.lv3: This is the controlled comparison in its cleanest form, and it is worth noticing what the engine holds constant for free that a real bench does not: identical starting temperature, identical heat loss (none), identical purity, identical stirring. A simulated fair test is trivially fair, which is precisely why the *habit* has to be taught here and the *difficulty* has to be met at a real bench. The virtual lab can teach the logic of control; it cannot teach the discipline of it.

setup.script:
add v1 water 100mL
add v1 HCl 0.1mol
add v1 NaOH 4g
new
add v2 water 100mL
add v2 NaOH 4g
add v2 HCl 0.1mol

predict.question: Sodium hydroxide pellets can go straight into the acid — one violent step — or dissolve in water first and then meet the acid, two milder ones. Which route ends up hotter?
options: The one-step route — doing everything at once releases the energy together
The two-step route — two separate heats add up to more
Neither: both beakers end at exactly the same temperature
predict.misconception: Enthalpy is a state function: the heat released between the same start and the same finish does not depend on the route taken between them. That is Hess's law, and both wrong answers imagine the route mattering — in opposite directions. The drama differs (one jump against two climbs); the destination cannot.

diagnosis.reveals: Intensity mistaken for total: one dramatic step 'releases more' than two mild ones, as if energy rewarded doing everything at once.
diagnosis.next: Watch both thermometers: 49.20 °C and 49.20 °C. The journeys differ — one beaker jumps in a single violent step, the other climbs twice, pausing at 35.7 °C as pH 13.51 lye water — but the destination is fixed by the two endpoints, not by the path drawn between them.

diagnosis.reveals: Heats counted per event rather than per change of state: two warmings must surely sum to more than one.
diagnosis.next: Add the second route's two heats up: the dissolution's warmth plus the mixing's, and the sum is the one-step release exactly. Energy is bookkept between states, and both routes connect the same two states — that the parts sum to the whole is the entire content of the law.

registers.lv1: Straight into the acid, or dissolve first and mix after — take either road. The thermometer ends on the same mark both ways. The heat doesn't care which road you took; only where you started and where you stopped.
registers.lv2: Hess's law: enthalpy is a state function, so the same reagents reaching the same final beaker release the same total heat, in any number of steps. Both routes read 49.20 °C — the dissolution's −44.5 kJ/mol and the neutralisation's ≈−56 kJ/mol are both paid, in different orders, into the same total — and the bench's energy balance conserves enthalpy through every intermediate state, so the agreement is exact rather than approximate.
registers.lv3: Both the law and the magnitude are computed, and the neutralisation enthalpy is read rather than curated: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O is the reverse of the reaction that defines OH⁻ in every shipped database, so its ΔH comes from the data files themselves — wateq4f says −55.91 kJ/mol, minteq.v4 −55.81, pitzer −56.36, a half-kJ disagreement between datasets of exactly the kind `explain` exists to show. (The −57.3 kJ/mol that school tables quote is the strong–strong calorimetric figure with dilution effects included — a different measurement.) Two boundaries, stated: this counts only the water-forming step, so a weak acid's neutralisation would read about 2 kJ/mol too exothermic here, its dissociation enthalpy being folded into a real calorimeter's number but not into this one; and the final pH of 8.91 is the 8 × 10⁻⁶ mol excess of base (four grams of NaOH is 0.100008 mol) read at the 49.2 °C the beaker actually reached — K_w has moved with the temperature, which is `neutral-is-a-moving-target` arriving uninvited. The exactness of the path-agreement was expensive: enthalpy stopped being a state function three separate ways in this engine before it held (PLAN.md carries the chronicle), and this entry only became writable when the last of them was fixed.

predict.question: 10 g of chalk in a crucible. Put 1 kJ of heat in — enough to take it to 147 °C, hotter than boiling water. What comes out?
options: Quicklime and carbon dioxide — it decomposed
Hot chalk. Nothing else. The balance still reads 10.00 g
Some of it decomposes; the rest does not
predict.misconception: 'Heating causes decomposition' becomes a rule with no threshold attached, so any heating is expected to do something. Decomposition has a temperature, and below it the reaction does not go slowly — it does not go. This entry exists to be the null result that gives the next one its meaning.

diagnosis.reveals: Heating causes decomposition, threshold-free: 147 °C is impressively hot by kitchen standards, so chemistry must be happening.
diagnosis.next: Push it in stages and weigh between each: hotter, hotter, still 10.00 g — then past the threshold in `chalk-in-the-kiln`, where everything happens at once. The pair of entries is the lesson: thresholds are not gradual approaches to drama.

diagnosis.reveals: Reactions as dimmer switches: every temperature buys some fraction of the effect, so partial heat should give partial decomposition.
diagnosis.next: Read the balance to its last digit: 10.00 g, not 9.9-something. Below the temperature where CO₂'s pressure over the carbonate reaches the room's, the gas cannot leave at all — the equilibrium is a door, and this side of the threshold it is shut, not ajar.

registers.lv1: Chalk in a crucible over a flame, hot enough to burn you badly, and when it cools down it is still chalk. Same white powder, same weight on the balance. Heating is not a magic ingredient: it has to be enough heat, and 'enough' is a specific number for every substance.
registers.lv2: 1 kJ into 0.0999 mol of CaCO₃ at 81.9 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹ raises it by 122 K: 25 °C → 147.2 °C, and the bench confirms 147.21 °C. No CO₂ is evolved, no CaO appears, and the balance still reads 10.00 g. Calcium carbonate needs roughly 900 °C before the decomposition runs.
registers.lv3: The equilibrium partial pressure of CO₂ over calcite at 420 K is around 10⁻¹⁵ bar — vastly below the ambient 10⁻³·⁴ bar — so the thermodynamic driving force points the other way and the carbonate is the stable phase. The Gibbs minimiser is not switched off here; it is run and returns 'unchanged', which is a computed result and not an assumption. A learner can move the heat up and find the crossing themselves.

predict.question: Same 10 g of chalk, but eight times the heat — past 1000 °C. The crucible gets lighter. Where is the temperature at which chalk decomposes written down in this program?
options: In a table of decomposition temperatures the engine looks up
Nowhere — it is computed, from the point where the CO₂ pressure over the carbonate reaches the pressure in the room
It is hard-coded as 900 °C
predict.misconception: A simulator is assumed to be a lookup table with animation on top, so any number it produces is assumed to have been typed in by someone. This one was not: the same solve that says 147 °C changes nothing says 1000 °C changes everything, and neither answer was written down in advance. That is the difference between a model and a recording.

diagnosis.reveals: Simulation as recording: numbers come from tables someone typed, so somewhere in this program a decomposition-temperatures table is being consulted.
diagnosis.next: `explain` the vessel: the provenance names NASA thermodynamic polynomials and a Gibbs minimisation — no decomposition table exists to consult. The same solve that refused at 147 °C calcines at 1000 °C, having looked nothing up in between.

diagnosis.reveals: The sharper form of the same idea: a specific constant, hard-coded — someone wrote 900 in the source the way textbooks print it.
diagnosis.next: Ask what the threshold depends on and a hard-coded number falls apart: it is the temperature where CO₂'s equilibrium pressure over the solid crosses the pressure of the room, which is why the answer belongs to the *conditions* and not to chalk alone. `explain` shows the data it fell out of; the source has no 900 to find.

registers.lv1: Now the chalk really does change. It glows, then goes dull, and what is left is a different white powder that weighs much less — and if you drop water on it, it hisses and gets hot. This is how lime for mortar has been made for four thousand years, and the only thing you needed was a hot enough fire.
registers.lv2: 8 kJ takes 0.0999 mol of chalk to about 1000 °C, above the decomposition point. CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂: the carbon dioxide escapes and the balance falls from 10.00 g towards the mass of the quicklime alone. Every mole of chalk that decomposes gives up 44.009 g of gas and keeps 56.077 g of oxide — a loss of 44%.
registers.lv3: The threshold is not tabulated. The minimiser is handed the element budget of the vessel plus its share of the atmosphere and asked for the composition with the lowest Gibbs energy at the temperature the enthalpy balance settles at; calcite wins below the crossing and lime-plus-gas above it. Element balance is a hard constraint here rather than an aspiration: the solver refuses to return a composition whose atoms do not add up to the ones that went in, to within a part in a billion, and it will report a failure to converge rather than a composition that creates matter. That check is the reason this entry can quote amounts at all — an earlier version of the minimiser tested convergence on the size of its own correction step instead of on the residual, and quietly returned twice the carbon dioxide it started with.

predict.question: Weigh a magnesium ribbon: 1.20 g. Burn it completely and weigh the white ash. Commit to a number before you look.
options: Less than 1.20 g — burning uses things up
Exactly 1.20 g — mass is conserved
1.99 g — more than you started with
Nothing left to weigh — it all went up in smoke
predict.misconception: This is the classic, and most people get it wrong. Every fire anyone has watched leaves less than it started with — a log becomes a handful of ash — so 'burning destroys matter' is learned from the world before it is unlearned in a classroom. The ash is lighter because the carbon left as gas. Magnesium's oxide is a solid and stays in the crucible, so the oxygen it took from the air is on the balance too. Burning is combination, not destruction; the log is the misleading case.

diagnosis.reveals: Fire consumes — learned at every campfire before any classroom: burning spends matter, and ash is the leftover.
diagnosis.next: Burn it here and weigh: 1.99 g from 1.20. The campfire was not lying — its lost mass left as gas. This fire's product is a solid, so the oxygen it took stays to be weighed; `burning-makes-it-lighter` runs the campfire's own case for the comparison.

diagnosis.reveals: Conservation applied to the ribbon alone: the air has no line in the books, so what was weighed must be what remains.
diagnosis.next: Redraw the boundary around ribbon *plus air* and the books balance perfectly: the extra 0.79 g is oxygen that crossed it. The law was never in danger — it was applied one boundary too small.

diagnosis.reveals: The strongest form of the campfire lesson: burning is annihilation, and 'up in smoke' means matter genuinely ending.
diagnosis.next: Put a balance under every fire in this codex: something always remains or leaves *as something* — a gas with mass, an ash with mass. `mass-in-an-open-vessel` catches the leaving mass mid-flight; no ledger in this lab ever books to zero.

registers.lv1: It burns with a white light so fierce it hurts to look at, and leaves a powder that is whiter than the ribbon was. Put it back on the scales: it is heavier. Something came out of the air and joined it — the air is not nothing, and this is one of the few experiments where you can weigh that fact.
registers.lv2: 0.0494 mol of Mg (1.20 g ÷ 24.305) becomes 0.0494 mol of MgO, which is 1.99 g. The gain of 0.79 g is 0.0247 mol of O₂ at 31.998 g/mol, taken from the atmosphere. Mass is conserved across the whole system; the crucible is not the whole system, and the missing accounting is the air.
registers.lv3: The oxygen is drawn from a reservoir rather than the vessel inventory, which is why the vessel's mass rises — a deliberate modelling choice matching an open crucible. The adiabatic solve settles at 3042 K with the condensed oxide dominant; at that temperature MgO(g) and atomic Mg are thermodynamically present in the NASA data but negligible at 1 bar, so essentially all of the metal is recovered as weighable solid.

predict.question: 1.20 g of charcoal, burned completely in the same crucible that made magnesium heavier. What is on the balance afterwards?
options: 1.20 g — mass is conserved
More than 1.20 g, as with the magnesium
Essentially nothing — the crucible is empty
predict.misconception: Having just been taught that burning adds mass, learners over-correct and expect every fire to gain. Both fires gain oxygen; the difference is entirely whether the oxide is a solid or a gas. Magnesium oxide stays; carbon dioxide leaves. Nothing about conservation changed between the two experiments — only the phase of the product.

diagnosis.reveals: Conservation clamped to the crucible, from the other side this time: gases do not count as mass leaving, so the reading should hold.
diagnosis.next: Seal it and burn — Lavoisier's move: closed, the reading holds exactly; open, the CO₂ carries its mass out of the top. Same law both times, boundary drawn honestly once.

diagnosis.reveals: The previous lesson over-corrected into a new rule: burning adds oxygen, oxygen has mass, so every ash must be heavier — the product's phase has no place in the rule yet.
diagnosis.next: Grant the premise, then ask where the oxide *is*: MgO sits in the crucible; CO₂ is in the room. Both fires gained oxygen — weigh the leaving gas instead (`mass-in-an-open-vessel`) and carbon's gain reappears, airborne.

registers.lv1: The charcoal glows orange and then there is nothing left to weigh. It did the same thing the magnesium did — it joined with the air — but what it made was invisible and floated off. That is why bonfires look like destruction and why people believed for centuries that burning destroyed things.
registers.lv2: 0.0999 mol of C (1.20 g ÷ 12.011) becomes 0.0999 mol of CO₂ — 4.40 g of gas, all of it gone from the crucible, which reads 0.00 g. The system gained 3.20 g of oxygen and the vessel lost 1.20 g of carbon; the two experiments differ in the phase of the product and in nothing else.
registers.lv3: The adiabatic flame settles at 2216 °C against magnesium's 2769 °C, and the gap is not about which reaction is 'stronger' — carbon's ΔH per mole of O₂ is comparable — but about where the energy goes: the product here is a gas that carries it away in translational and vibrational modes, while magnesia is a condensed phase with far less to absorb. Flame temperature is an enthalpy balance, not a ranking of fuels.

predict.question: Two identical 1.2 g magnesium ribbons burn in identical air. One is barely warm when it catches (228 °C); the other is already glowing (927 °C). Do the two flames reach the same temperature?
options: Yes — the flame temperature is a property of magnesium
No: 2177 °C and 2769 °C. The heat you put in first is still in the products
No — the hotter one burns faster and so ends up cooler
predict.misconception: 'Adiabatic flame temperature of magnesium' gets memorised as a constant, like a melting point. It is not a property of the fuel; it is the answer to an enthalpy balance, and the enthalpy of the reactants is one of the inputs. Preheat the reactants and you get a hotter flame, which is exactly why industrial furnaces preheat their air.

diagnosis.reveals: Flame temperature as a substance constant, filed beside the melting point: one fuel, one number, whatever state it started in.
diagnosis.next: Change only the starting enthalpy and read the answer: 700 degrees more preheat, roughly 600 degrees more flame. A constant cannot respond to how you began; a balance must — and furnaces preheat their air because engineers bill by that balance.

diagnosis.reveals: Speed spends the heat: the hotter start burns faster, and faster somehow means the energy is used up sooner and ends cooler — rate entangled with the energy budget.
diagnosis.next: Adiabatic means the ledger keeps everything regardless of pace: same fuel, same oxygen, more starting enthalpy — more ending enthalpy, full stop. Rate decides how soon the products arrive at their temperature, never what that temperature is.

registers.lv1: Two identical ribbons, both burned, both blindingly bright — and one flame is six hundred degrees hotter than the other. The only difference was how warm the metal was when it caught. Heat you put in beforehand does not disappear when the fire starts; it is still there, added on top.
registers.lv2: Adiabatic means no heat leaves, so the products' enthalpy equals the reactants'. Starting at 228 °C the solve lands at 2176.97 °C; starting at 926.9 °C — the ignition temperature the bench uses — it lands at 2768.67 °C. Same ΔH of reaction, −601 kJ/mol; different starting enthalpy, different answer.
registers.lv3: The solver bisects on temperature until the products' enthalpy matches the reactants', evaluating both from the NASA-9 polynomials rather than assuming a constant heat capacity — which matters, because Cp rises substantially over two thousand kelvin. The vessel's share of the atmosphere is in the balance too, and it is the dominant heat sink: a gram of magnesium heats the air around it far more than it heats the speck of oxide it leaves.

predict.question: Magnesium and oxygen release 601 kJ per mole — thermodynamics says the metal should not exist in air at all. Two ribbons are heated: one to 224.3 °C, one to 228.4 °C. What happens?
options: Both burn — the reaction is favourable at both temperatures
Neither burns — 228 °C is nowhere near hot enough
Only the second burns. Four degrees is the difference between nothing and everything
The first burns slowly, the second quickly
predict.misconception: 'The reaction releases energy, so it happens' is the single most common conflation in chemistry, and the last option is its softer form — the belief that an unfavourable rate means a slow reaction rather than no reaction. Equilibrium says where a system would end up; it says nothing about whether it can get there. A magnesium ribbon in a drawer is thermodynamically desperate to become oxide and will sit there for a century, because an oxide skin stands in the way.

diagnosis.reveals: Thermodynamics as sufficiency: released energy means it happens — the barrier between here and the favourable end state has no place in the picture.
diagnosis.next: The four-degree experiment is the barrier made visible: 224.3 °C, nothing; 228.4 °C, everything. Favourability did not change by so much as a joule between those two readings — access did.

diagnosis.reveals: Ignition as extremity by definition: a couple of hundred degrees feels too tame for a metal to catch, so the threshold is imagined somewhere far away and dramatic.
diagnosis.next: Run it: 228 °C is past this ribbon's threshold, and from there it climbs to over 2000. Thresholds sit where the balance puts them, not where drama suggests — which is why this entry asks you to commit to a number first.

diagnosis.reveals: Rate as a dial that never reads zero: everything happens at some speed, so 'unfavourable' can only mean slow — 'does not go' is not an available answer.
diagnosis.next: Watch the cooler ribbon for as long as you like: no smoulder, no creeping mass gain on the balance — nothing. The ribbon in a drawer for a century is the long version of the same run; the oxide skin is not slowing the reaction down, it is standing in its way.

registers.lv1: Two identical ribbons. Heat one to 224 °C and it is just a hot ribbon. Heat the other four degrees further and it erupts into a two-thousand-degree fire. Nothing about the metal or the air changed — there is a line, and everything depends on which side of it you are.
registers.lv2: Equilibrium says magnesium in air should be magnesium oxide at every temperature: ΔH = −601 kJ/mol and ΔG is negative throughout. It is not, because a coherent oxide layer stops oxygen reaching the metal. The bench encodes that with an explicit threshold at 500 K (226.85 °C): below it the thermal solver stands down and leaves solids alone, and 224.29 °C leaves 1.20 g of metal while 228.4 °C gives 1.99 g of oxide.
registers.lv3: This threshold is an admitted stand-in, not a kinetic model. The engine computes equilibrium and equilibrium would oxidise every metal on the bench instantly; a real treatment needs activation energies, an Arrhenius rate and a diffusion model for the passivating layer, which is an L5 concern and not wired. The honest move is to make the boundary a named constant a learner can read — KINETIC_THRESHOLD_K — rather than to let equilibrium quietly lie about the world. Do not read 226.85 °C as magnesium's ignition temperature; read it as the engine saying 'kinetics lives here and I do not model it'.

provenance.source: Standard treatment of thermodynamic versus kinetic control; the passivating-oxide explanation is textbook corrosion chemistry. That the engine's 500 K threshold is a placeholder for kinetics rather than a measured ignition temperature is Editorial judgement (Kerotakis), read from the solver's own documented constant.. predict.question: Hold a flame to 5.00 g of potassium chloride. The flame turns lilac. What does the balance read afterwards, and what is the temperature of the salt?
options: Lighter, and hot — some of it burned off to make the colour
5.00 g and 25 °C. Nothing burned; the colour is light, not fire
Heavier — it combined with oxygen like the magnesium did
predict.misconception: A coloured flame looks like combustion, so the salt is assumed to be the fuel. It is not: the flame excites the potassium's outer electron and the colour is what that electron emits falling back. Nothing is consumed, and a flame test on a milligram will keep going as long as you hold it there. This is also the entry that shows what a negative result looks like — three things that did not happen, each of which is checked.

diagnosis.reveals: Colour is combustion's receipt: if it glows, something is being spent — light without fuel is not in the picture.
diagnosis.next: Weigh and take the temperature afterwards: 5.00 g, 25 °C — a negative result with every negative checked. The lilac is an electron falling back to its shelf, not matter leaving; a milligram would colour the flame for as long as you cared to hold it there.

diagnosis.reveals: The magnesium template, pattern-matched onto any solid in a flame: metal-ish thing plus fire equals oxide plus mass gain.
diagnosis.next: Ask what would have to change for the template to apply: potassium chloride's ions are already in their stable states, with nothing to offer oxygen. The flame test works *because* nothing reacts — which is what lets it identify an element without destroying the sample.

registers.lv1: Hold the salt in a flame and the flame turns lilac — a completely different colour from the same burner a moment earlier. Weigh the salt: unchanged. Touch it once it is out of the flame: cold. You have identified the metal without using any of it up, which is why this test is nearly two hundred years old and still in use.
registers.lv2: The bench reports a flame test and nothing else: no ignition, no consumption, no gas. 5.00 g in, 5.00 g out, 25.00 °C before and after. Potassium gives lilac, sodium gives yellow, calcium orange-red — the colour identifies the cation, and the anion is invisible to the test.
registers.lv3: Two separate things are being asserted, and they come from different places. That nothing burns is computed: the Gibbs minimiser finds no exothermic path and the bench restores the vessel exactly. That the flame is lilac is curated spectroscopy — potassium's 766.5/769.9 nm doublet plus the violet lines — because the thermodynamic databases hold no electronic-transition data and the lab does not invent any. Worth noticing too: the equilibrium composition contains traces of Cl₂ at the nanomole level, and the bench refuses to announce them, because a trace is not an observation.

predict.question: Dissolve 5.844 g of salt in 100 mL of water — the basin reads 105.54 g. Boil the water away. What does the basin read now?
options: 0 g — it all evaporated
5.84 g — the salt is left behind
105.54 g — mass is conserved
Less than 5.84 g — some salt goes with the steam
predict.misconception: Young learners often think dissolving destroys the salt, so nothing should remain; older ones, having learned conservation, apply it to the basin and expect the whole 105.54 g. The measurement that settles it is the pair — before and after, on the same balance — which is why you write the first number down before you start rather than after you see the second.

diagnosis.reveals: Dissolving destroyed the salt, so boiling merely finishes the disappearance — what vanished from sight vanished from existence.
diagnosis.next: Boil it and look in the basin: 5.84 g of crystals, the mass that went in, back on the same balance. `particles` shows where the salt was the whole time — out of sight was never out of the ledger.

diagnosis.reveals: Conservation pinned to the basin: the reading is the system, so the whole 105.54 g must survive the boiling.
diagnosis.next: Weigh what left: 99.7 g of water is now vapour in the room, carrying its mass with it. The before/after pair on one balance is precisely the instrument for catching a boundary drawn wrong — which is why the first number is written down first.

diagnosis.reveals: Evaporation as a general carrier: whatever is in the liquid rides out with the vapour, brine and all.
diagnosis.next: Check what the vapour can hold: at these temperatures the salt's ions have no route into the gas, which is why evaporating seawater is how salt is *made* — and why kettle scale stays stubbornly behind rather than steaming away.

registers.lv1: The salt vanished into the water and you cannot see it any more. Boil the water off and there it is again, the same amount as you started with. It was never gone — and the way you know, rather than believe, is that you wrote down the weight beforehand and can compare.
registers.lv2: 105.54 g before, 5.84 g after: 99.70 g left as water vapour, which is the 100 mL of water at 0.997 g/mL. The salt recovered, 5.84 g, is the 5.844 g put in — a recovery of 99.9%. Amount of substance is conserved through the dissolving and the evaporating; only the water went anywhere.
registers.lv3: Nothing about this is trivial in the engine: the aqueous solver held 0.1000 mol of Na⁺ and 0.1000 mol of Cl⁻ in solution, and evaporation to dryness has to hand them back as solid NaCl without losing a mole. A useful boundary to try afterwards: evaporate in two steps rather than one and the bench emits 'not yet modelled' — solid salt in contact with the last film of liquid is a regime no wired solver owns. The single-step path is clean; the two-step path is honest about not being.

predict.question: Two things vanished on this bench: salt disappeared into water, and a magnesium ribbon disappeared into flame. Which of the two can you undo?
options: Both — chemistry can always be run backwards if you are clever enough
Neither — once a substance is gone, it is gone
Only the salt: boil the water away and the crystals return; no amount of heating or cooling un-burns the ribbon
predict.misconception: The two disappearances are the same event to the eye and opposite events underneath. The salt is still sodium chloride, hiding as ions — remove the water and it must come back. The ribbon's atoms are all still there too, but in new company: magnesium oxide is a new substance, and temperature cannot dissolve a chemical bond that heat itself favours. Telling these two vanishings apart is the definition of a chemical reaction.

diagnosis.reveals: Reversibility as cleverness rather than as a property of what happened — dissolving and reacting filed as the same kind of vanishing, undone by the same kind of trick.
diagnosis.next: Try both on this bench: evaporate the brine and the crystals return, mass ledger intact. Heat the ash, cool it, wait at it — magnesium oxide it stays. Undoing it takes a new chemical partner and a great deal of energy (industry does it by electrolysis of the molten salt), not a cleverer application of heat.

diagnosis.reveals: Dissolution as destruction — the young learner's default: the salt is gone the way the ribbon is gone, and gone is gone.
diagnosis.next: The balance never agreed: the brine weighs the salt the whole time (`weigh-before-and-after`), and evaporation hands it back as crystals you can count in grams. The two vanishings differ in what remains — the same substance hiding, or a new substance formed — and that difference is the whole content of the words 'chemical reaction'.

registers.lv1: The salt hid in the water — boil the water away and there it is again, white and sharp-cornered. The ribbon did not hide: it *became* something new, and no amount of un-heating brings it back. That is the difference between mixing something and really changing it.
registers.lv2: Dissolving is a physical change: NaCl(s) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq), reversed by removing the solvent — evaporate 95% of the water and 0.069 mol of crystals return, the rest still dissolved in the last 5 mL. Burning is a chemical change: 2 Mg + O₂ → 2 MgO, a new substance with new properties, and no temperature reverses it.
registers.lv3: Both halves are computed, and both carry their fine print. The brine at 95% evaporated holds 0.0692 mol of solid salt beside 0.031 mol still in solution — solubility stays a ratio to the remaining water down to the last millilitre, which is `crystallising-salt-from-brine`'s subtraction taken nearly to its end. The ash side: the thermal solver answers 'magnesium oxide' at every temperature this bench can reach, because the oxide is downhill from the metal everywhere — reversing it is not a temperature question but an electron question, which is why industry electrolyses the molten chloride instead of heating the oxide. One boundary named: evaporating to *total* dryness currently leaves the final trace of ions labelled aqueous with no water to be aqueous in — a state the registry has no story for yet — which is why this entry stops at 95%.

predict.question: Two beakers, both above the solubility product, so silver chloride forms in both. In the first the amount formed is 0.16 µmol; in the second it is 1.7 µmol. What does the bench report?
options: A precipitate in both — the chemistry is the same
A precipitate in neither — both are far too dilute to see
A precipitate in the second only: the first is below the observation floor of 1 µmol
predict.misconception: The unstated assumption is that whatever the chemistry does, the experiment shows. Every instrument has a floor, and below it a real change produces no signal — which is not the instrument lying, it is the instrument having a specification. Confusing 'I did not detect it' with 'it did not happen' is how a negative result gets over-read, and the fix is knowing your detection limit before you run.

diagnosis.reveals: The experiment shows whatever the chemistry does — instruments as transparent windows, with no floor of their own.
diagnosis.next: Read the specification this bench publishes about itself: the observation floor is one micromole. The first beaker's 0.16 µmol is real, in the ledger, and below the floor — 'not shown' and 'not there' are different sentences, and an honest instrument says which one it means.

diagnosis.reveals: The right instinct, uncalibrated: detection limits exist, but they sit wherever caution imagines them — and both amounts 'feel' invisible.
diagnosis.next: The floor is a number, not a mood: 1 µmol here. 1.7 sits above it and is reported; 0.16 sits below and is named rather than shown. Knowing the limit *before* the run is what turns 'nothing seen' into information instead of a shrug.

registers.lv1: Two beakers with almost unmeasurably small pinches of chemical. Something really does happen in both. Only one of them shows you anything. Every measuring device has a smallest thing it can notice, and below that it says nothing at all — which is not the same as there being nothing.
registers.lv2: Both mixtures exceed Ksp(AgCl) ≈ 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰, so solid forms in both. In v1 only about 0.16 µmol can form, below the bench's 1 µmol observation floor, and no precipitation event is emitted; in v2 about 1.7 µmol forms and the event fires. Inspecting v1 still shows silver chloride in its inventory — the bookkeeping is exact and only the reporting is floored.
registers.lv3: The floor is OBSERVABLE_MOLES = 10⁻⁶ mol, applied uniformly to precipitation, dissolution and gas evolution. It is a deliberate stand-in for an instrument specification: a real turbidimeter, a real nose and a real balance all have limits, and a simulation that announces every nanomole trains a learner to expect a sensitivity no bench possesses. The number is a modelling choice, not a measured constant, and it is worth saying out loud that a nephelometer would see AgCl well below it while an eye would not see it well above.

provenance.source: Ksp and speciation from PHREEQC wateq4f.dat (USGS). That a uniform 10⁻⁶ mol reporting floor is the right stand-in for an instrument's detection limit is Editorial judgement (Kerotakis), and the engine's own documented rationale.. predict.question: Gypsum is stirred into acetone instead of water. What should a chemistry program do?
options: Dissolve it — it dissolved in water, so it dissolves
Say 'not yet modelled': no wired solver covers this salt in a non-aqueous solvent
Crash with an error
Silently leave the salt at the bottom, as if that were the computed answer
predict.misconception: Software is expected to answer. The tempting failure is the last option — quietly doing nothing and letting silence be read as a result, which is indistinguishable from 'it is insoluble' and happens to be roughly right here, for entirely the wrong reason. A model that cannot tell you where it stops has told you nothing you can trust anywhere.

diagnosis.reveals: Solubility belongs to the salt alone: it dissolves, full stop — the solvent is interchangeable scenery rather than half of every dissolution.
diagnosis.next: Name what the solver actually knows: water's behaviour, from a thermodynamic database about water. Gypsum in acetone is in fact essentially insoluble — but the bench refuses to claim even that without a curated row that knows it, which is the difference between being right and being lucky.

diagnosis.reveals: Software has exactly two states, answer or error: a stated 'I don't know' is not in the vocabulary, so the only alternative to answering is breaking.
diagnosis.next: Run it: `not_yet_modelled` arrives as a first-class result, with provenance, and the CI fails any lesson that goes silent instead of saying it. The third state is this program's entire premise — a model that can name its own edge.

diagnosis.reveals: The subtlest one: silence read as an answer. A program that does nothing has 'said' the salt is insoluble — and being roughly right hides that nothing was computed at all.
diagnosis.next: This exact defect sits in the project's own history: 'nothing ignited' once meant 'no solver engaged', reported as if it were a fact about ethanol. The rule it forced — wherever the engine declines to model something, it says so — is in PLAN.md, and this entry is that rule in teaching form.

registers.lv1: Ask the lab something it does not know and it tells you it does not know. It does not guess, and it does not pretend the silence was an answer. Knowing the edge of what you know is part of knowing anything at all — and a person who can say 'I have not got a method for that' is more useful than one who always has a number.
registers.lv2: The aqueous engine's databases are parameterised for water: activity models, solubility products and speciation are all built on aqueous standard states. Acetone is a liquid the bench can hold and pour, and for some solutes in some organic solvents a curated handbook row now answers (NaCl's near-insolubility in ethanol, CaCl2's high solubility in acetone, for two) — but for this salt in this solvent no row exists yet, so the honesty pass emits 'not yet modelled' rather than a number. The balance still works — the acetone plus the salt — because mass bookkeeping is not the thing in doubt.
registers.lv3: The event is `NotYetModeled`, raised by the honesty pass when a solid coexists with a liquid and no solver — and no curated verdict — covers the pair. It is structurally different from `SolverFailed`, which means a wired solver tried and did not converge. This entry originally demonstrated the gap with NaCl in ethanol, then moved to CuSO4 in ethanol — both of which the curated organic-solubility rung (CAP-23) now covers with handbook data. As coverage grows, the demonstration moves to the next uncovered pair; model boundaries move, and an honest bench moves its examples with them. This paragraph is the record that it happened.

provenance.source: Editorial judgement (Kerotakis): the design decision to emit a stated gap rather than a guess, and the argument for teaching model boundaries as content, is ours. Diagnoses: Editorial judgement (Kerotakis), drafted with model assistance (Claude, 2026-08-20, updated 2026-08-24)
