predict.question: A lump of zinc sits in iron(II) sulfate solution. What happens — and why do steel ship hulls carry bolted-on zinc blocks?
options: Nothing; zinc and iron are too similar to bother each other
Iron metal plates out while the zinc dissolves — zinc gives its electrons first, which is exactly the sacrifice the hull block makes
The zinc rusts instead of the iron, because rust prefers the more reactive metal
predict.misconception: The third answer has the right instinct dressed in the wrong mechanism: nothing 'prefers' — zinc simply sits below iron in the series, so wherever electrons are demanded, zinc pays before iron does. In this beaker that means dissolved iron is pushed back to metal at zinc's expense; on a hull it means the corrosion current drains the replaceable block instead of the irreplaceable plate. Same ordering, same sacrifice.

diagnosis.reveals: Similar metals, no chemistry: reactivity differences are imagined to need drama — acid against metal, not grey against grey.
diagnosis.next: The gap only has to be nonzero: −0.76 V against −0.45 V is enough for every last iron ion here. `inspect` afterwards: 0.0100 mol of iron plated out, the zinc gone into solution — a third of a volt, fully spent.

diagnosis.reveals: Rust as an agent with preferences, hopping to the more reactive metal — protection imagined as decoy behaviour rather than as electron bookkeeping.
diagnosis.next: Replace 'prefers' with a direction: electrons flow from the lower metal up to whatever is being reduced. The zinc block corrodes *because* it is the electron source of least resistance — no preference, just the same ordering that made iron plate out in this beaker.

registers.lv1: The zinc lump slowly gives itself away, and grey iron fur grows where it stood. On a ship it is the same trick: bolt on a lump of zinc and the sea eats the lump instead of the hull — a bodyguard that takes the hit on purpose.
registers.lv2: Zn + Fe²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Fe (E° −0.76 V below −0.45 V): 0.0100 mol of iron plates onto the dissolving zinc. Sacrificial protection is this reaction run as a maintenance plan — the zinc is cheaper to replace than the steel it guards.
registers.lv3: This is P3e's 'why zinc protects iron', answered by computation rather than assertion: the direction falls out of the same Nernst comparison as every other pairing in the series. Honesty notes: real hull protection is an electrochemical cell with oxygen at the cathode, richer than this single beaker; and the fresh iron chemistry here sits near known engine boundaries (a supersaturation this registry cannot name may be reported), so this entry pins amounts and pH, not potentials.

add v1 Zn 0.05mol

add v2 Cu 0.05mol

predict.question: Zinc stands in zinc sulfate, copper in copper sulfate, a salt bridge between them and a voltmeter across the metals. What does the meter read?
options: 0 V — the metals never touch, so no chemistry connects them
About 1.1 V — the distance between the two metals' rungs on the series
About 0.4 V — the average of the two electrode potentials
predict.misconception: A voltage is a *difference*, not an average and not a contact: each metal sits at its own electrode potential against its own ions, and the meter reads the gap — E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) − E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = 0.34 − (−0.76) ≈ 1.10 V. The displacement reaction and the battery are the same chemistry: put the metals in one beaker and the electrons jump directly as heat; separate the half-cells and the same electrons must take the wire, where they can be made to work.

diagnosis.reveals: Reaction requires contact: the metals never meet, so nothing can happen — the circuit as a whole is not yet the unit of chemistry.
diagnosis.next: Follow one electron's options: it leaves the zinc either directly onto a Cu²⁺ at the metal's surface (`the-series-decides-who-plates`, which turned the gap into 218.7 kJ/mol of heat) or through the wire to the copper electrode, doing the same chemistry at a distance. The salt bridge closes the loop of charge; the wire is where the trade becomes measurable.

diagnosis.reveals: Potentials are averaged rather than subtracted — two numbers on a chart combine the way marks on a test do.
diagnosis.next: Check the sign convention against the beaker: the meter reads which way electrons *want* to flow, and a want is a difference. The bench prints the arithmetic with the verdict: E° +0.342 minus −0.762 gives the 1.104 V it reports, electrons offered from v1 to v2.

registers.lv1: Two jars, two metals, a paper bridge of salt water, and a meter between them: it reads a real voltage — a battery made of nothing but the two metals' different appetites for electrons.
registers.lv2: Zn | Zn²⁺ ‖ Cu²⁺ | Cu: E = E°(cathode) − E°(anode) = 0.34 − (−0.76) ≈ 1.10 V, and the bench reads 1.104 V open-circuit. This is Daniell's cell of 1836 — the displacement reaction of `the-series-decides-who-plates` with the two halves separated, so the electrons take the wire.
registers.lv3: Open-circuit, and the bench says so: this is the voltage the cell *offers*, not what it delivers under load — current would drop it by internal resistance and polarisation, neither modelled here, and the report states as much. The 1.104 V is Nernst over the activities PHREEQC computes for each side (E° alone gives 1.1037; the two 0.01 mol/kgw solutions nearly cancel each other's corrections). Both half-cells sit within half a degree of 25 °C at these amounts — at 0.1 mol the dissolution heat would put the two electrodes at different temperatures, which is why this entry uses the dilute version.

predict.question: The textbook exercise: dilute the copper side of a Daniell cell tenfold, and E falls by 0.0592/2 volts per decade — 29.6 mV. The bench dilutes and reads the meter. By how much did the voltage actually fall?
options: Exactly 29.6 mV — the Nernst equation is an equation
18.2 mV — noticeably less, because the free copper activity fell by a factor nearer 4 than 10
Nothing — dilution changes how much copper there is, not what copper is
predict.misconception: The Nernst equation IS exact — over activities. The slide-rule version quietly substitutes concentrations, which assumes the activity corrections cancel between the two solutions. They do not: in the stronger solution much of the copper is paired with sulfate, so tenfold less total copper is only about fourfold less *free* Cu²⁺, and the logarithm sees the four. The second witness clinches it: a copper–silver cell reads 0.445 V at 0.01 mol but 0.483 V at 0.1 — the deviation changes sign with concentration, so no 'always a bit less' patch-rule survives.

diagnosis.reveals: The equation as printed is the physics: concentrations go into the log because that is where the book put them — the activity footnote never made it into working memory.
diagnosis.next: This lab has taught the same lesson three times with different meters: `ph-is-not-quite-minus-log-c` (the pH electrode), `half-oxidised-iron-reads-its-own-potential` (the redox electrode), and now the whole cell. Look at v2's lv3 speciation: the CuSO₄ ion pair holds a third of the copper, and the pinned engine test asserts the drop is less than ideal rather than any particular number — the deviation is the chemistry.

diagnosis.reveals: Voltage as identity: what a metal 'is' sets its potential, and amount is bookkeeping — the log term has no physical meaning attached.
diagnosis.next: Run the strongest counterexample first (`a-battery-from-nothing-but-imbalance`): two identical copper electrodes, nothing different but the concentration, and a real 18 mV appears. If amount didn't move potentials, that cell would read zero forever.

registers.lv1: Water down one side of the battery and its push gets weaker — but less weak than the rule of thumb promised. The beaker knows something the slide rule doesn't: how much of the copper is really free.
registers.lv2: E = E° − (0.0592/2)·log(a(Zn²⁺)/a(Cu²⁺)). Tenfold less total copper should cost 29.6 mV if concentration were activity; the bench reads 1.104 → 1.086 V, a drop of 18.2 mV, because sulfate pairing means the free-Cu²⁺ ratio between the two solutions is nearer 4 than 10.
registers.lv3: The fails_at of the concentration-form Nernst, written as chemistry: in molar-strength sulfate media the ion pair CuSO₄(aq) carries a large share of the copper, and the share *changes with dilution*, so no fixed correction rescues the concentration form. The engine's regression test deliberately asserts an inequality (drop < ideal) rather than 18.2 mV, because the honest claim is the mechanism, not this scenario's number. The copper–silver pair supplies the sign-flip witness (0.445 V at 0.01 mol, 0.483 V at 0.1, against E° 0.458): at low concentration the n=1 silver term dominates the deficit, at high concentration the sulfate-starved copper term overpowers it.

predict.question: Same metal both sides, same salt both sides — copper in copper sulfate twice, only the concentration differing tenfold. The voltmeter reads…
options: 0 V — identical electrodes cannot disagree about anything
About 18 mV, with the dilute side as the negative pole
About 1.1 V — two beakers and a bridge make a Daniell cell whatever is in them
predict.misconception: The standard potentials cancel identically — E° = 0.000, and the bench prints it — yet a real voltage remains, because the Nernst term reads the imbalance itself: the dilute side dissolves copper to gain ions and the strong side plates copper to shed them, the cell literally running on the urge to even out. A battery needs a difference, and a difference in concentration is a difference.

diagnosis.reveals: Potential belongs to the substance: identical metals, identical potentials, zero forever — concentration has no seat at the electrode.
diagnosis.next: Read the bench's own arithmetic: E° = 0.000 exactly, E = 0.018 V anyway. The whole reading is the log term — cover the E° column of the table with your thumb and this cell works exactly the same, which no cell built on 'the metals differ' can say.

diagnosis.reveals: Any two beakers wired up make 'the battery from the book' — the apparatus is the cause, and 1.1 V is what apparatus of this shape produces.
diagnosis.next: The 1.104 V belonged to a specific pair of rungs, not to the glassware (`the-daniell-cell-offers-its-voltage`). Same glassware, same bridge, copper both sides: sixty times less voltage. The series sets the big number; here the series contributes nothing and the leftover is pure Nernst.

registers.lv1: Two jars of the same blue water — one strong, one weak — copper in both, bridge between. The meter still reads something! The strong side wants to give copper away, the weak side wants more: wanting-to-even-out is enough to make electricity.
registers.lv2: Cu | Cu²⁺(0.001) ‖ Cu²⁺(0.01) | Cu: E° cancels to 0.000 and E = (0.0592/2)·log(a₂/a₁) — the bench reads 0.018 V with the dilute side as anode. A concentration cell is the Nernst equation with everything else subtracted out.
registers.lv3: The cleanest 'the number is the activities' witness this bench can stage: no table value survives into the answer, so the 18.4 mV is entirely the computed activity ratio (which is why it is not the ideal 29.6/2-per-decade value either — the same pairing correction as `dilution-buys-less-than-the-slide-rule-says`). The direction is the second lesson: the *dilute* side is the anode, dissolving its own electrode to catch up — matter moving to erase a gradient, read out in volts. Nerve cells and pH electrodes run on this identical principle.

setup.script:
add v1 water 100mL
add v1 CuSO4 0.05mol
add v1 Cu 0.01mol
electrolyse v1 0.5A 1930s

predict.question: Half an ampere runs for 1930 seconds through copper sulfate — 965 coulombs, almost exactly a hundredth of a faraday. How much copper lands on the cathode?
options: 0.0100 mol — one mole of electrons deposits one mole of metal
0.0050 mol — every copper ion demands two electrons
No saying without the voltage — volts are what drive electroplating
predict.misconception: The chain is Q = It, n(e⁻) = Q/F, n(metal) = n(e⁻)/z, m = nM — and three of those four steps are pure arithmetic. The divisor z is the single piece of chemistry in it: Cu²⁺ takes two electrons, so a hundredth of a faraday buys half a hundredth of copper. Voltage decides whether the deposition runs at all; the charge decides how much, to four figures.

diagnosis.reveals: Electrons and atoms pair one-to-one — the ion's charge, the only chemical input in the whole calculation, is the step that got skipped.
diagnosis.next: Run the zinc twin: the same 965 C into zinc sulfate deposits the same 0.0050 mol — 0.327 g against copper's 0.318, differing only by molar mass — because both ions are 2+. Then imagine silver: the same charge would deposit 0.0100 mol, since Ag⁺ takes one. The electron count sets the moles; the ion's charge is the exchange rate.

diagnosis.reveals: Voltage as the quantity dial: more volts, more metal — the roles of the two electrical quantities are merged into 'electricity'.
diagnosis.next: Separate them the way the meter does: voltage is the pressure that decides whether Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu runs; charge is the count of electrons that actually crossed, and every single one is accounted for in the deposit. Faraday weighed exactly this in 1833 — the balance as an electron counter.

registers.lv1: Wire a battery to the blue bath and copper grows on the wire — and it grows by strict bookkeeping: run the current twice as long, get exactly twice the copper. Electricity is countable stuff, and the metal counts it for you.
registers.lv2: Q = 0.5 A × 1930 s = 965 C → n(e⁻) = Q/F = 0.0100 mol → n(Cu) = 0.0050 mol → m = 0.318 g. Dose it: 120 C gives 0.040 g, 3600 C gives 1.185 g — mass tracks charge through the whole series.
registers.lv3: Only the 2 is chemistry: the bench reads the divisor off the couple the vessel holds rather than being told, and the rest is arithmetic a learner can check by hand — which is the entry's point. Boundaries, stated by the bench where they bite: charge beyond what the solution's copper can absorb stops at the supply with the note that a real cell would electrolyse the water instead; and brine is refused outright, because chlorine chemistry is not modelled — the chlor-alkali cell, the most famous industrial electrolysis of all, is a named gap rather than a wrong answer.

setup.script:
add v1 water 100mL
add v1 CuSO4 0.05mol
add v1 Cu 0.01mol
electrolyse v1 0.5A 1930s

predict.question: You electroplate 0.318 g of copper out of the blue bath. What happens to the bath's pH?
options: Nothing — plating moves metal, and metal is not acid
It crashes, from 4.3 to 1.8: every Cu²⁺ removed left its charge behind, and the anode pays the bill in protons
It rises — taking the metal out 'frees up' the solution
predict.misconception: Charge conservation runs the show: every Cu²⁺ that leaves the solution as metal takes two positive charges out of the water, and the solution cannot simply go negative. At the inert anode the books are balanced by oxidising water itself — 2 H₂O → O₂ + 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻ — so oxygen bubbles away and acid accumulates, one proton per electron. Nobody expects electroplating to acidify the bath, and it falls straight out of the ledger.

diagnosis.reveals: The cathode is the whole story: metal moves there, so that is where the chemistry is — the anode is just the other wire.
diagnosis.next: Follow the electrons the cathode consumed back to their source: they came out of water molecules at the anode, and each departure left a proton. The bench books it exactly — 0.0025 mol of O₂ leaves the open vessel, the water inventory drops from 5.5342 to 5.5292 mol, and the pH lands at 1.84. A circuit has two ends, and both of them do chemistry.

diagnosis.reveals: Solutes as burden: removing anything 'frees' the solution and moves it toward pure water's 7 — dissolved copper and acidity filed as the same kind of impurity.
diagnosis.next: Check what was actually removed and what was created: the copper left, but its counter-charge did not — sulfate stays, and new H⁺ arrived to face it. The bath ends as dilute sulfuric acid, which is why industrial plating shops monitor and dose their baths instead of trusting them to self-purify.

registers.lv1: Plate the copper out and the bath turns sour — sharp enough to sting. The bubbles at the other wire are the clue: the water itself is being taken apart to pay for the copper you removed.
registers.lv2: Cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Anode (inert): 2 H₂O → O₂↑ + 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻. Per 0.0100 mol of electrons: 0.0050 mol copper deposited, 0.0025 mol oxygen out, 0.0100 mol H⁺ made — pH 4.27 → 1.84.
registers.lv3: Which anode is the load-bearing choice, and the bench names its own: the *inert* anode (the school's carbon rods), where water is oxidised and acid accumulates. A *copper* anode dissolves to replace exactly what plates out — Cu²⁺ constant, no acid, no oxygen — and that different cell is electrorefining, which this bench does not model. Same cathode, opposite bath chemistry, decided entirely at the electrode you were not watching.

setup.script:
add v1 water 100mL
add v1 ZnSO4 0.01mol
add v1 Zn 0.05mol
new
add v2 water 100mL
add v2 CuSO4 0.01mol
add v2 Cu 0.05mol
cell v1 v2
electrolyse v1 0.5A 386s
add v1 HCl 0.05mol

predict.question: The Daniell cell offers 1.104 V, spending zinc as it discharges. What is 'charging' — the thing that makes an accumulator rechargeable?
options: Refilling it with electricity, which it stores the way a tank stores fuel
Using an outside current to run the cell's own reaction backwards, rebuilding the metal that discharging consumed
Replacing the used-up chemicals with fresh ones
predict.misconception: A battery stores no electricity — it stores a chemical reaction held ready to run. Discharging lets the reaction run downhill through the wire; charging is an outside supply forcing the same reaction uphill, re-depositing the anode metal electron by electron (193 C here rebuilds 0.0010 mol of zinc, by the same Faraday arithmetic as any electrolysis). The tank picture fails at exactly the point that matters: what is stored is a chemical arrangement, not a substance called electricity.

diagnosis.reveals: Electricity as a stored fluid: charge goes in, sloshes about, comes back out — the oldest model of electricity, and inside a battery it is wrong in a way that matters.
diagnosis.next: Weigh the electrodes across a cycle instead of imagining the tank: discharging thins the zinc, charging thickens it back — matter moves, which no stored-fluid picture predicts. The bench shows the rebuild directly: 193 coulombs in, 0.065 g of zinc back on the metal.

diagnosis.reveals: Rechargeable and disposable batteries differ by service regime: someone, somewhere, swaps the chemicals — regeneration by current is not in the picture.
diagnosis.next: Nothing enters the cell but electrons: the 'fresh chemicals' are the old ones, pushed back up the hill they ran down. That is the whole distinction from a primary cell — an accumulator's chemistry is reversible in place, which is also why its electrodes must survive being rebuilt a thousand times.

registers.lv1: Push the current backwards and fresh zinc grows onto the metal — and it stays there, even though the sour bath would love to eat it, because making hydrogen bubbles on zinc is hard work. That hardness is the battery's bodyguard. Overwhelm it with too much acid and the bodyguard loses: fizz, and your stored charge leaves as gas.
registers.lv2: Discharge: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, offering 1.104 V. Charge: an external supply drives Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn against the series — 193 C = 0.0020 mol of electrons rebuilds 0.0010 mol (0.0654 g) of zinc while the inert anode acidifies the bath to pH 2.13. And the deposit holds: dissolving it would need hydrogen to form on zinc, and that costs ~0.72 V of overpotential against a driving force of only +0.69 V. Pour in strong acid and the barrier is cleared: Zn + 2 H⁺ → Zn²⁺ + H₂, 0.026 mol of gas, the charge undone.
registers.lv3: The bench's own verdict is the entry's thesis, verbatim: 'zinc should dissolve in this acid by the series (driving force +0.69 V), but hydrogen has to form on zinc, and on that surface it costs an overpotential of about 0.72 V. Kinetically blocked on the timescale of a lesson, not thermodynamically inert — the difference between a bench and a battery.' That 0.03 V of grace is why rechargeable cells exist — on zinc here, on lead in every car battery — and gassing on overcharge is precisely the leash slipping, staged in this script's final act with molar acid. Honesty, three ways: the overdriven margin clears by only 0.07 V because the bath's own sulfate and chloride speciation holds a(H⁺) below one (at a true pH 0 it would be 0.04 V), and a rate that close to its barrier is not computed — the bench says 'it reacts, slowly' and claims no more; the overpotential itself is a curated kinetic constant, not a computed one; and the cell and electrolysis remain uncoupled — nothing here computes discharge under load, internal resistance or capacity, so 'a cell run backwards' is a statement about half-reactions, not runtime.

provenance.source: Standard curriculum accumulators (charge as reverse reaction); hydrogen overpotential on zinc ~0.72 V curated (standard electrochemistry), applied as a kinetic gate on the series' verdict; the sulfate/chloride activity effects computed. setup.script:
add v1 water 100mL
add v1 HCl 0.1mol
add v1 Pb 0.02mol
new
add v2 water 100mL
add v2 Pb(NO3)2 0.01mol
add v2 Zn 0.02mol

predict.question: A car battery is lead plates standing in strong acid, for years. Lead sits below hydrogen in the activity series, so the acid should dissolve it. Why doesn't it?
options: The series is simply wrong about lead
Kinetics: hydrogen formation on lead costs about 0.88 V of overpotential, far more than the +0.13 V the acid offers — blocked, not absent
The plates get a protective factory coating that keeps the acid off
predict.misconception: When an observation contradicts a rule, the tempting moves are to discard the rule or to invent a protector. Neither is needed: the series is an equilibrium statement and it is right — lead in acid is downhill. It is also barely downhill (+0.13 V), and the reaction's necessary first product, hydrogen gas on a lead surface, carries an activation toll of ~0.88 V. The bill exceeds the budget, so the reaction is blocked on any human timescale. The battery exists inside that gap.

diagnosis.reveals: Rules are right or wrong, never bounded: one contradicting observation and the series is discarded, rather than asked what it actually claims.
diagnosis.next: Test the series where no kinetic gate applies: v2 — lead plates out of its own ions onto zinc, 0.0100 mol, exactly the direction the ordering demands. The series is right about where equilibrium lies; it never claimed to be a clock, and this beaker pair is the difference.

diagnosis.reveals: Inertness needs an agent: 'nothing happens' must be caused by a thing — a coating, an additive — rather than by a barrier in the reaction's own mechanism.
diagnosis.next: No coating is modelled and none is invoked: the barrier is the surface chemistry of forming H₂ on lead itself, and the bench states the arithmetic — +0.13 V offered, ~0.88 V demanded. A century and a half of lead-acid batteries stands on that gap, not on a factory step.

registers.lv1: A car battery is metal standing in strong acid — for years on end. The acid would love to eat the lead, but making gas bubbles on lead is so hard that nothing happens at all. The battery exists because of that nothing.
registers.lv2: v1: lead in acid is reported inert — driving force +0.13 V against ~0.88 V of hydrogen overpotential on lead; no gas, no dissolution, pH unmoved. v2: the same series still works when kinetics allows it — Zn below Pb, so 0.0100 mol of lead plates onto the dissolving zinc.
registers.lv3: The comparison with zinc is the design lesson: zinc's grace is 0.03 V (`charging-fights-the-series` slips that leash with molar acid); lead's is ~0.75 V — the widest safe margin of any cheap metal below hydrogen, which is why lead was THE accumulator metal for a hundred and sixty years. Honesty: the overpotential is a curated kinetic constant with 'timescale of a lesson' as its stated scope, and the verdict here rests on it alone — real lead in sulfuric acid additionally grows a lead-sulfate film this bench does not model, so the real battery is even better protected than this beaker.

setup.script:
add v1 water 100mL
add v1 NaCl 0.1mol
new
add v2 water 100mL
cool v1 15kJ
cool v2 15kJ

predict.question: Two identical beakers lose the same heat side by side: one holds pure water, the other has a big spoon of salt dissolved in it. What differs?
options: Both, at 0 °C — freezing at zero is what water does
The salty one first — salty water is thicker, and thicker is closer to solid
The pure one starts at 0 °C; the brine starts near −4 °C and therefore makes less ice from the same cooling
predict.misconception: The first answer makes the freezing point a fixed property of the solvent, with the dissolved salt as cargo that changes nothing. It is a property of the solution: the ions get in the way of water ordering itself into an ice lattice, so the brine must be colder before freezing pays. The same removed energy consequently makes less ice in the brine. The 'thicker' answer runs viscosity and solidity together — how a liquid flows and whether its molecules can lock into a crystal are different questions with opposite answers here.

diagnosis.reveals: The freezing point belongs to the solvent, full stop — what is dissolved is cargo, riding along without a vote.
diagnosis.next: Count the cargo's votes: about 1.86 °C of hold-out per mole of dissolved particles per kilogram of water, and salt splits largely into two ions — 0.1 mol of NaCl in 100 g of water is roughly 2 mol/kg of particles. The bench reads the actual particle count off the solved speciation and starts freezing the brine near −4 °C, which is why road grit is dosed in degrees.

diagnosis.reveals: Thickness as nearness to solid: a heavier, saltier liquid feels half-way frozen already, so it should finish freezing first.
diagnosis.next: Separate the two ideas: flow is about how molecules slide past each other; freezing is about whether they can lock into a lattice. The dissolved ions obstruct the lattice, so more salt means the beaker holds out longer, not less — the saltier you make it, the colder it must get before ice pays.

registers.lv1: The plain water starts freezing at zero. The salty water holds out until about four degrees below zero, so the same cooling makes less ice there — the salt gets in the way of the ice forming. That is the secret of gritting icy roads.
registers.lv2: Freezing-point depression: ΔT ≈ 1.86 K·kg/mol × molality of dissolved particles. 0.1 mol of NaCl in 100 g of water is 1.0 mol/kg of salt but roughly 2.0 mol/kg of dissolved particles, so the brine starts freezing about 4 K below pure water. As pure ice forms, the salt stays in the residual liquid; the bench re-solves that more concentrated brine and its lower liquidus.
registers.lv3: The depression is computed from the solved speciation — the same particle census `particles` draws — rather than from an integer van 't Hoff factor. Only as much water freezes as the withdrawn 15 kJ can pay for, latent heat counted, and the inventory keeps liquid water and pure ice side by side. Each ice transfer invalidates the old molalities, so PHREEQC re-speciates the smaller liquid compartment and the phase pass iterates to a common temperature/liquidus. Below the declared 252 K model boundary, salt solids and a solute-specific eutectic phase diagram would be required; the bench stops rather than extrapolating the dilute colligative relation.

provenance.source: Standard curriculum colligative properties; freezing-point depression computed from the solved speciation (PHREEQC via Kerotakis L2) by the Kerotakis state layer; cryoscopic constant of water 1.86 K·kg/mol is a standard reference value quoted for comparison. Diagnoses: Editorial judgement (Kerotakis), drafted with model assistance (Claude, 2026-08-20)

models.name: Particle model (Teilchenmodell)
models.power: Lets you predict that matter is conserved when it appears to vanish — the sugar that dissolves, the puddle that dries — and to order the three states as one substance in three arrangements rather than as three substances. It is the first model that makes an invisible cause explain a visible effect.
explains: dissolving without any loss of mass
the three states of matter and every change between them
diffusion: why a smell crosses a room with nobody carrying it
why gases can be compressed and liquids and solids cannot
thermal expansion
why a solution is clear rather than cloudy
fails_at: Cannot say WHY sodium and chlorine react, only that they do — the particles have no parts to rearrange.
Has no answer to why one substance is a metal and another a gas: every particle is the same featureless sphere.
Cannot explain why oil and water refuse to mix, because it gives particles no way to attract each other differently.

Taken literally it invites the classic error of attributing macroscopic properties to single particles — a hot particle that expands, a copper particle that is orange — and of filling the space between particles with air.
models.embodied_by: kerotakis-core's vessel inventory. A vessel is nothing but a list of (species, moles, phase); dissolving salt moves an amount from the solid phase to the aqueous one and the ledger is unchanged. The particle model's central claim is enforced as a data structure and checked by a 256-case conservation property test.

registers.lv1: Everything is built from pieces far too small to see, and they never stop jiggling. In a solid they are packed tight and can only wobble; in a liquid they slide past each other; in a gas they fly apart with nothing but empty space between them. When sugar disappears into tea it has not gone anywhere — the pieces have slipped into the gaps between the water pieces, which is why the tea still tastes sweet and still weighs exactly the same.
registers.lv2: Matter consists of discrete particles (Teilchen) in constant motion, separated by empty space. Temperature measures their mean kinetic energy, and the states of matter differ in how much of that energy is available against the forces holding the particles together. Melting, boiling, dissolving and diffusion are all rearrangements of the same particles, so none of them changes the mass.
registers.lv3: The kinetic particle model — the school ancestor of kinetic gas theory. It is purely mechanical: particles have mass, volume and velocity and nothing else, which is precisely why it yields Boyle's and Gay-Lussac's laws and not one chemical fact. In Johnstone's terms it is the first submicroscopic model a learner meets, and it is not spontaneously acquired: continuous-matter intuitions persist for years, learners fill the inter-particle space with air, and they transfer macroscopic properties onto individual particles.

provenance.source: Standard curriculum; documented misconceptions from Novick & Nussbaum, Junior high school pupils' understanding of the particulate nature of matter: an interview study, Science Education, 1978, and Andersson, Pupils' conceptions of matter and its transformations (age 12-16), Studies in Science Education, 1990

models.name: Dalton's atomic model (Atommodell nach Dalton)
models.power: Turns stuff into countable, indestructible units with a fixed mass per element, which is what makes a chemical formula and a balanced equation possible at all. With Dalton you can predict the mass ratio in which two elements combine before you run the experiment.
explains: conservation of mass in a reaction
the law of constant proportions: every sample of water has the same composition
the law of multiple proportions: CO and CO2 but never CO1.5
the difference between element, compound and mixture
why a chemical equation must balance
fails_at: The atom is a solid indivisible sphere, so there is nothing that can be transferred: ions, charge, electrolysis and electricity are all outside the model.
All atoms of an element are identical is simply false — isotopes exist, and are the reason chlorine's relative atomic mass is 35.45 rather than a whole number.
Says nothing about why elements fall into families, so the periodic table has to be memorised rather than derived.
Atoms that cannot be divided cannot decay, so radioactivity has no place in it.
models.embodied_by: The Gibbs minimiser (kerotakis-cea). Its constraint is one Lagrange multiplier per element, so every state it finds conserves atoms exactly — methane burns to CO2 and water with elements conserved to 1e-6. Dalton's claim is not an assumption inside the solver; it is the constraint the solver optimises under.

registers.lv1: Every substance is built from a small number of kinds of building block called atoms, and each kind has its own weight. Atoms are never made and never destroyed — a reaction only takes them apart and puts them together differently, like rebuilding a Lego model from the same bricks. That is why nothing ever weighs less afterwards.
registers.lv2: Elements consist of atoms; all atoms of one element share a mass; compounds contain atoms in fixed whole-number ratios; a reaction rearranges atoms without creating or destroying any. From this follow conservation of mass, the law of constant proportions and the law of multiple proportions — carbon and oxygen give CO and CO2, never anything between.
registers.lv3: Dalton (1808) is the first model here that is quantitative and predictive rather than descriptive, and the law of multiple proportions is its genuine prediction, made ahead of the evidence. It also carried an instructive error: the rule of greatest simplicity assigned water the formula HO, which put the whole atomic-mass table wrong until Avogadro's hypothesis and Cannizzaro's intervention at Karlsruhe separated atom from molecule. That fifty-year gap is the clearest available case of a model right in its structure and wrong in a parameter.

provenance.source: Dalton, A New System of Chemical Philosophy (1808); Avogadro (1811); Cannizzaro, Sunto di un corso di filosofia chimica (1858), circulated at the Karlsruhe Congress in 1860

models.name: Nuclear model (Kern-Hülle-Modell, Rutherford)
models.power: Splits the atom into two parts with different jobs: a tiny heavy nucleus that fixes identity and mass, and an outer electron region that does all the chemistry. That single split is what makes ions, charge, radioactivity and the distinction between a chemical and a nuclear change explainable at all.
explains: the alpha-scattering experiment: most particles pass, a few bounce back
that an atom is almost entirely empty space
ions as atoms that have lost or gained electrons
electrolysis and electrical conduction in solutions
isotopes: same nuclear charge, different mass
why no chemical reaction ever changes which element you have
fails_at: A classical orbiting electron radiates and would spiral into the nucleus in about 10^-11 s. The model predicts that no atom can exist, which is the sharpest failure in the whole progression.
The shell has no structure, so it cannot say why the noble gases are inert or why sodium loses exactly one electron.
It predicts a continuous emission spectrum; glowing hydrogen actually gives a handful of sharp lines.
models.embodied_by: The species registry is keyed by composition and charge, and the aqueous solver works entirely in ions — Na+ and Cl- are separate entries with separate thermodynamics. Nothing anywhere in the engine changes a nucleus: a chemistry solver is by construction a model of the shell alone.

registers.lv1: Fire tiny bullets at a sheet of gold foil and almost all of them go straight through as if nothing were there — but about one in ten thousand bounces straight back. So an atom must be mostly empty space with something very small, very heavy and positively charged right in the middle: the nucleus. Everything else is a cloud of light, negative electrons around it. Rub a balloon on your hair and you are stealing some of them.
registers.lv2: Rutherford (1911), from Geiger and Marsden's alpha scattering: an atom has a nucleus of protons and neutrons carrying essentially all the mass in roughly a hundred-thousandth of the diameter, surrounded by Z electrons. The nucleus fixes which element it is; only the shell takes part in chemistry. Removing or adding shell electrons gives ions, and ions are the raw material of all salt chemistry.
registers.lv3: This is where chemistry and physics separate cleanly: nuclear charge Z is identity, the electron shell is chemistry. It is also the model whose failure is quantitative and unambiguous — an accelerated charge radiating by the Larmor formula collapses the atom in about 10^-11 s — which is why the next step had to be a postulate against classical mechanics rather than a refinement of it. Presented with that failure named, Bohr's stationary states stop looking arbitrary.

provenance.source: Rutherford, The scattering of alpha and beta particles by matter and the structure of the atom, Philosophical Magazine, 1911; Geiger & Marsden, 1909. The classical-collapse lifetime is the standard textbook estimate from the Larmor radiation formula

models.name: Shell model (Schalenmodell, Bohr)
models.power: Puts electrons in numbered shells of fixed capacity, and that one move makes the periodic table derivable instead of memorised: group number is the count of outer electrons, period number is the shell being filled, and the octet rule then tells you which ion an element forms before you have ever seen it react.
explains: the line spectrum of hydrogen, quantitatively
why the noble gases are unreactive
the ion charges of the main groups, and hence salt formulae
why sodium and potassium behave alike
ionisation energy rising across a period and jumping between shells
flame colours as electrons falling back between shells
fails_at: Predicts the wrong spectrum for anything bigger than hydrogen. Helium, with two electrons, already has no solution and the model's numbers are simply wrong.
Cannot explain why the 4s shell fills before 3d, which is why the transition metals refuse to fit the tidy shell story.
Electrons run on circles, so molecules have no shape: it cannot say why water is bent at 104.5 degrees or methane tetrahedral.
No fine structure, and no account of lines splitting in a magnetic field.
It is a hybrid — classical orbits with a quantum rule bolted on — and nothing inside the model justifies the rule.
models.embodied_by: Only as curated data, and that is worth saying out loud. The lab's flame test shows sodium's yellow from a colour table, not from a computed transition — the very prediction Bohr is famous for is one this engine asserts rather than calculates.

registers.lv1: Electrons are not just anywhere. They live in layers around the nucleus, like the rings of an onion, and each layer has room for only so many. An atom is content when its outside layer is full, and that is the whole secret of chemistry: atoms give away, take, or share electrons until everyone's outer layer is full. Heat an atom and an electron jumps up a layer, then falls back and gives out light of one exact colour — which is why salt turns a flame yellow.
registers.lv2: Bohr (1913): electrons occupy shells K, L, M, N with capacities 2, 8, 18, 32 (that is 2n squared). Energy is emitted or absorbed only when an electron changes shell, and E = hf gives hydrogen's sharp lines. The number of electrons in the outermost shell is the valence, and the octet rule — the drive to a noble-gas configuration — then predicts Na+ and Cl-.
registers.lv3: Bohr quantises angular momentum by postulate and reproduces the Rydberg formula exactly for one-electron systems, E = -13.6 eV / n squared. That success is confined to H, He+ and Li2+; helium fails outright, because a postulate about single orbits has nowhere to put electron-electron repulsion. Sommerfeld's elliptical orbits patched the fine structure without curing the disease. The model survives in school because valence-shell counting is genuinely useful, but the planetary image it plants is documented to persist into university, and this engine's registers should never draw an atom as a solar system.

provenance.source: Bohr, On the constitution of atoms and molecules, Philosophical Magazine, 1913; persistence of the planetary-orbit image documented in the conceptual-change literature, e.g. Taber, Building the structural concepts of chemistry, Chemistry Education Research and Practice, 2001

models.name: Charge-cloud model (Kugelwolkenmodell, Kimball)
models.power: Gives molecules a shape. Once the outer electrons are four repelling clouds rather than dots on a circle, the tetrahedron falls out, and a learner can predict from the formula alone that methane is tetrahedral, ammonia pyramidal and water bent — and that each lone pair squeezes the angle further.
explains: the tetrahedral carbon atom, and hence the whole shape of organic chemistry
bond angles of 109.5, 107 and 104.5 degrees in methane, ammonia and water
why water is a dipole and carbon dioxide is not, despite both having polar bonds
the difference between bonding pairs and lone pairs
single, double and triple bonds as one, two or three shared clouds
fails_at: Every cloud is the same size and shape, so there is no s and no p, no subshells, and no way to say why an atom's outer electrons differ in energy at all.
The photoelectron spectrum of methane shows two different valence ionisation energies, not four identical ones: the four equivalent bonds the model draws are not what the experiment sees.
Transition metals break it. d electrons do not fit a four-cloud picture, and neither does an octahedral complex with six ligands.
It cannot describe delocalisation: benzene comes out as two alternating structures, neither of which exists, and metals and conjugated dyes are outside it entirely.
It is a geometry model with no spectroscopy and no energies in it — no ionisation energies, no colour, no bond strengths.

registers.lv1: Electrons go around in pairs, and each pair sits in its own little round cloud. The clouds push each other away, so they spread out as far as they can get. Four clouds around a carbon atom end up pointing at the four corners of a pyramid shape — and that really is the shape of methane. Water has two clouds doing the bonding and two just sitting there taking up room, which is why water is bent instead of straight.
registers.lv2: Kimball's charge clouds (Kugelwolken): each electron pair occupies a spherical cloud, clouds repel, and they take the arrangement of maximum separation — two linear, three trigonal planar, four tetrahedral. Lone pairs need more room than bonding pairs, so the H-O-H angle is 104.5 degrees rather than 109.5. A double bond is two clouds shared between the same pair of atoms.
registers.lv3: The German school Kugelwolkenmodell descends from G. E. Kimball's charge-cloud picture and is, in modern terms, a localised sp3 electron-pair model with the mathematics removed; it is a close cousin of VSEPR (the Elektronenpaar-Abstoßungsmodell) and of Linnett's double-quartet. Its value is real — correct main-group geometry from a rule a fourteen-year-old can apply — and its cost is that it presents localised pairs as physical objects, which makes delocalisation, photoelectron spectra and metallic bonding all look anomalous instead of expected.

provenance.source: Standard German curriculum (Kugelwolkenmodell); the underlying charge-cloud picture is G. E. Kimball's, and its close relative VSEPR is Gillespie & Nyholm, Quarterly Reviews of the Chemical Society, 1957. Editorial judgement (Kerotakis): placing the Kugelwolkenmodell between Bohr and the orbital model follows German didactic practice rather than the historical order, since Kimball's work postdates Schrödinger's

models.name: Orbital model (Orbitalmodell)
models.power: Replaces where the electron is with how likely it is to be there, and in doing so becomes the first model of the atom that is calculated rather than postulated. It gives the aufbau order and hence the shape of the periodic table including the d and f blocks; it gives molecular orbitals and hence bond order, magnetism and colour; and it is the only model in this progression whose error can be systematically reduced instead of patched.
explains: the aufbau principle, Pauli exclusion and Hund's rule
the s, p, d and f block structure of the periodic table
why 4s fills before 3d
why liquid oxygen sticks to a magnet: two unpaired electrons in pi-star orbitals
delocalisation, aromaticity and the colour of dyes
HOMO and LUMO, and hence where a molecule is attacked
fails_at: There are no orbitals in a many-electron atom. An orbital is a one-electron function; the true wavefunction of even helium is not a product of them, so the 2p orbital of oxygen is an approximation being spoken of as an object.
The Schrödinger equation has an exact solution for one electron only. Everything past hydrogen is an approximation whose accuracy has to be argued for rather than assumed.

A single-determinant orbital picture cannot even break the bond in H2 correctly at long distance, which is the simplest case of the static correlation that defeats it across transition-metal and excited-state chemistry.
As usually taught it is non-relativistic, so it gets gold's colour and mercury's liquidity wrong.
It is not a model a learner can compute with: the predictions come out of software, so it buys explanation rather than hand calculation.
models.embodied_by: Nothing at runtime, deliberately. PLAN.md confines quantum chemistry to build time (L4'): orbital shapes would ship as precomputed meshes, never as a live calculation, and the honest runtime ceiling is a qualitative Hückel tier. No orbital is computed anywhere in the shipped engine, because thermodynamics does not need one.

registers.lv1: Nobody can say exactly where an electron is — only where it is likely to be. So instead of a ring, picture a fuzzy cloud around the nucleus, thicker where the electron spends more of its time. Different clouds have different shapes: some are balls, some look like two balloons tied together. The shapes are the reason atoms join up pointing in particular directions instead of just anywhere.
registers.lv2: Electrons occupy orbitals — solutions of the Schrödinger equation labelled n, l and m — and the square of the wavefunction gives the probability density. Orbitals fill by the aufbau principle, the Pauli exclusion principle and Hund's rule, which reproduces the periodic table block by block. When atoms combine, atomic orbitals overlap into bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals; bond order is half the difference between them, and O2's two unpaired antibonding electrons are why liquid oxygen is paramagnetic.
registers.lv3: The orbital model is the one-electron (Hartree-Fock) approximation to the many-body problem: orbitals are basis functions of an approximation, not physical containers. What distinguishes it in kind from every earlier model here is that it comes with a theory of its own error and can be improved systematically — post-Hartree-Fock, density functional theory, multireference methods. The pedagogical hazard is the mirror image of Bohr's: learners who successfully abandon orbits often reify orbitals instead and treat them as places. This is also where school chemistry's models end and computational chemistry begins, which is why Kerotakis draws its line here.

provenance.source: Schrödinger, Annalen der Physik, 1926; aufbau, Pauli and Hund per standard quantum chemistry (e.g. Atkins & Friedman, Molecular Quantum Mechanics). Learner reification of orbitals documented by Taber, Learning quanta: barriers to stimulating transitions in student understanding of orbital ideas, Science Education, 2005

models.name: The periodic law (Periodensystem der Elemente)
models.power: Compresses the properties of a hundred-odd elements into two coordinates. Group and period alone let you predict an element's ion charge, its formula with oxygen and chlorine, whether it is a metal, roughly how reactive it is and roughly how large its atoms are — for elements you have never met. Mendeleev's gaps show it is genuinely predictive rather than a filing system.
explains: why the alkali metals, the halogens and the noble gases each behave as a family
trends in atomic radius, ionisation energy and electronegativity
valency, and hence the formula of an unfamiliar oxide or chloride
Mendeleev's prediction of eka-silicon, found as germanium in 1886
fails_at: Ordering by atomic mass — Mendeleev's own criterion — puts tellurium after iodine and argon after potassium, both wrong. The law only became exact when Moseley replaced mass with nuclear charge in 1913.
The trends are trends, not laws: aluminium's ionisation energy is below magnesium's and oxygen's below nitrogen's, and only the orbital model explains the exceptions.
It orders without explaining. Nothing in the table says why a period ends where it does; the shell model supplies that, and the d and f blocks need orbitals.
Hydrogen has no home in it, and the lanthanides and actinides are printed underneath because they will not fit the page.

registers.lv1: Line the elements up in the right order and the same kinds of behaviour keep coming round again, like the days of the week. Everything in the first column is a soft metal that fizzes in water; everything in the last column does nothing at all. Once you know which column something is in, you can say a great deal about it before you ever open the jar.
registers.lv2: Elements ordered by atomic number fall into 18 groups and 7 periods. The group number gives the number of valence electrons and hence the usual ion charge — group 1 gives +1, group 17 gives -1 — and the period number gives the shell being filled. Atomic radius falls left to right and grows down a group; ionisation energy and electronegativity do the opposite. Mendeleev (1869) left gaps and predicted the density and melting point of the missing eka-silicon; germanium turned up in 1886 and matched.
registers.lv3: Periodicity is a consequence, not an axiom: it follows from the aufbau filling of shells and subshells, and the period lengths 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32 are the 2n-squared degeneracies sliced by the filling order. Mendeleev's ordering by mass was empirically right and theoretically wrong; Moseley's 1913 X-ray work established that the true ordinal is nuclear charge, which fixed the tellurium-iodine inversion and fixed how many elements were still missing. Take the table as the archetype of this codex's thesis: a model whose whole value lies in ordering rather than in any fact it contains.

provenance.source: Mendeleev, 1869 (Journal of the Russian Chemical Society; German abstract in Zeitschrift für Chemie); Moseley, The high-frequency spectra of the elements, Philosophical Magazine, 1913. Editorial judgement (Kerotakis): treating the periodic law as a model in its own right, rather than as a table of facts to be consulted, is our framing

models.name: Ionic bonding (Ionenbindung)
models.power: Predicts from the periodic table alone which pairs of elements form a salt and what its formula will be — and, because the model is a three-dimensional lattice of alternating charges rather than a pair of partners, it predicts the whole property profile at once: hard, brittle, high-melting, insulating as a solid and conducting once molten or dissolved.
explains: electron transfer from metal to nonmetal, and the ions that result
the formula of a salt from the ion charges: NaCl, MgCl2, Al2O3
why salts melt high and are hard
why a struck salt crystal cleaves cleanly instead of denting
why solid salt does not conduct but molten or dissolved salt does
dissociation into mobile ions on dissolving
fails_at: There is no fully ionic bond. Even NaCl has measurable covalent character, and by AlCl3 the salt has stopped being one: it sublimes at 180 degrees as covalent Al2Cl6 molecules.
Complete transfer implies a dissolved salt is a gas of independent ions, and the engine's own answer disagrees — ion pairs and neutral complexes such as AgCl(aq) are really there.
It cannot give a number. The lattice energy comes from a Born-Haber cycle, which is thermodynamics, not the transfer picture.
It says nothing about which salts dissolve. Sodium chloride and silver chloride are both ionic; one goes in by the spoonful and the other does not.
models.embodied_by: The aqueous solver works in ions throughout — a dissolved salt enters the calculation as element totals and comes back as a distribution of species. It also demonstrates the model's boundary rather than describing it: the neutral AgCl(aq) complex appears in the computed speciation, so the fully-separated-ions picture is visibly incomplete on screen.

registers.lv1: A metal atom has one or two electrons it barely holds on to. A nonmetal atom badly wants one more. So the metal simply hands them over. Now one is positive and the other negative, and opposite charges pull — but not just in pairs: millions of them stack into a rigid grid, plus, minus, plus, minus, in all directions. That grid is a salt crystal. Hit it and it does not dent, it splits, because sliding the grid by one step puts plus next to plus and it flies apart.
registers.lv2: A metal transfers valence electrons to a nonmetal; both reach a noble-gas configuration and become ions. Electrostatic attraction in every direction builds an ion lattice (Ionengitter), not molecules — NaCl is a formula unit, not a particle. The lattice explains the properties: strong non-directional forces give high melting points, displacement along a lattice plane puts like charges together and the crystal cleaves, and charge can only flow once the ions are free to move.
registers.lv3: The ionic bond is the limiting case of a bond with maximal charge separation; its energy is dominated by the Madelung sum with a Born repulsion term, and Born-Haber cycles show that lattice energies calculated on a purely ionic model agree well for alkali halides and progressively worse as polarisability rises — Fajans's rules summarise the drift. In solution the picture must be relaxed further: PHREEQC returns ion pairs and neutral complexes, so the fully dissociated ideal is a dilute-solution approximation, and its activity corrections are exactly what the codex surfaces at lv3.

provenance.source: Standard curriculum; Born-Haber cycle and Madelung treatment per standard inorganic chemistry; Fajans's rules for the covalent drift. Speciation and ion pairing computed by Kerotakis L2 (PHREEQC, USGS databases)

models.name: Covalent bonding (Atombindung / Elektronenpaarbindung, Lewis)
models.power: Lets you draw a molecule you have never seen from its formula alone: count the valence electrons, share them into pairs until every atom has a noble-gas configuration, and read off the number of bonds and the lone pairs. Almost all of organic chemistry is downstream of that one piece of bookkeeping.
explains: H2, Cl2, HCl, H2O, CH4, NH3 and every simple molecule
single, double and triple bonds, and why they get shorter and stronger in that order
why nonmetals with nonmetals give molecules rather than lattices
why molecular substances melt low and do not conduct
formal charge, and how to choose between competing structures
fails_at: Lewis structures make O2 a tidy double bond with every electron paired, and therefore predict it to be non-magnetic. Liquid oxygen sticks to a magnet: it has two unpaired electrons, and only molecular-orbital theory gets this right.
Benzene needs two structures that both do not exist plus a rule that reality lies in between; the model has no way to draw one delocalised system.
The octet rule is broken by BF3, PCl5, SF6 and every free radical. A rule with that many exceptions is a heuristic.
There are no energies in it: it cannot say whether a bond is strong, or whether a reaction will release heat.

registers.lv1: Two atoms that both want more electrons cannot both take, so they share instead. Each puts in one electron and the pair sits between them, holding them together like two children gripping the same rope. Share two pairs or three and the grip is stronger and shorter. Substances built this way come as separate little molecules with hardly anything holding one molecule to the next, which is why they melt so easily and never carry electricity.
registers.lv2: Nonmetal atoms reach a noble-gas configuration by sharing electron pairs. Shared pairs are bonding pairs, unshared ones are lone pairs, and Lewis notation makes the count explicit: eight valence electrons per atom, two for hydrogen. Bond order rises and bond length falls from C-C to C=C to C-triple-bond-C. The strong attraction is inside the molecule, so melting and boiling — which only separate molecules from each other — happen at low temperatures.
registers.lv3: Lewis (1916) predates quantum mechanics and remains the most used model in chemistry, because electron-pair bookkeeping is an extraordinarily good approximation for main-group compounds. Its real status is that of a localised-bond approximation to the molecular-orbital description, valid wherever that description happens to be localisable; where it is not — O2's triplet ground state, benzene, hypervalency, radicals, metals — the failures are systematic, not incidental. Note also that the d-orbital account of SF6 taught in school books is disfavoured in the modern computational literature in favour of ionic-covalent resonance with little d participation.

provenance.source: Lewis, The atom and the molecule, Journal of the American Chemical Society, 1916; Langmuir (1919) for the octet terminology; the case against d-orbital hypervalency from the natural-bond-orbital literature (Reed & Weinhold; Magnusson)

models.name: Metallic bonding (Metallbindung, Elektronengasmodell)
models.power: Explains a metal's entire property profile from one picture — fixed positive cores in a sea of mobile electrons. Electrical and thermal conduction, lustre, and above all malleability: a lattice held together by a shared electron sea can be deformed without breaking, which is exactly what an ionic lattice cannot do.
explains: electrical conduction in a solid metal
thermal conduction
malleability and ductility, against the brittleness of salts
metallic lustre
alloys as one metal lattice with another metal's atoms mixed in
why metals form cations and never anions
fails_at: It predicts every metal to conduct, and has no way to describe a semiconductor or an insulator — silicon sits between the two and the electron sea cannot say why. That needs band theory.
Nothing in the sea sets a bond strength, so it cannot explain why mercury is liquid at room temperature while tungsten melts at 3400 degrees.
It gets colour wrong by omission: copper and gold are not silver-grey, and the reason is relativistic band structure.
Superconductivity, magnetism and the way resistance changes with temperature are all outside it.
models.embodied_by: Only at its edges, which is itself informative. The engine treats a metal as a pure condensed phase with NASA-9 thermodynamic data and, in solution, as a cation — a magnesium ribbon is an inventory item with a heat capacity until it burns. Nothing in Kerotakis models the metallic state itself — and since 2026-08-20 the bench announces this boundary in the beaker at the moment it matters (a metal dropped into a salt solution says that displacement is not modelled), rather than only documenting it here where the learner most likely to be misled would never look.

registers.lv1: In a metal the atoms let go of their outermost electrons, which then wander freely through the whole lump — a kind of electric glue that is everywhere at once. Because the glue is not between fixed partners, you can hammer the metal flat and it holds together instead of shattering. And because the loose electrons can travel, they carry electricity and heat from one end to the other.
registers.lv2: Metal atoms release their valence electrons into a delocalised electron gas (Elektronengas); the resulting cations (Atomrümpfe) sit in a close-packed lattice bound by their attraction to that gas. Mobile electrons carry current and heat. The bond is non-directional, so layers of cations can slide past one another without ever bringing like charges together — metals deform where ionic solids cleave.
registers.lv3: This is Drude's free-electron gas (1900), corrected by Sommerfeld with Fermi-Dirac statistics — without which the model predicts an electronic heat capacity roughly a hundred times too large. Even corrected it cannot produce a band gap: the metal / semiconductor / insulator distinction requires the periodic lattice potential, Bloch's theorem and band structure. School chemistry stops at the sea because band theory belongs to solid-state physics, and naming that boundary is what stops the electron sea being mistaken for the last word.

provenance.source: Standard curriculum (Elektronengasmodell); Drude, Annalen der Physik, 1900; Sommerfeld's Fermi-Dirac correction (1928); band theory from Bloch, Zeitschrift für Physik, 1929

models.name: Electronegativity and the bond triangle (Elektronegativität, Bindungsdreieck)
models.power: Replaces three separate bond types with one continuous map. Two numbers — the difference in electronegativity and its average — place any binary compound inside a triangle whose corners are ionic, covalent and metallic, so the question stops being which type is it and becomes how far towards each corner. On the way it predicts bond polarity, hence molecular dipoles, hence solubility and where a molecule gets attacked.
explains: polar covalent bonds and partial charges
why HCl is polar and Cl2 is not
why CO2 has polar bonds and no dipole while water has both
the gradient from NaCl through AlCl3 to SiCl4
why the metals sit bottom-left and the nonmetals top-right of the periodic table
the reactive site of a carbonyl group
fails_at: Electronegativity cannot be measured. Pauling, Mulliken and Allred-Rochow define it differently and give different numbers, and the difference-above-1.7-is-ionic rule is a convention: HF has a difference of 1.9 and is a covalent gas.
It is a property of an atom in a molecule, not of a free atom. The same element pulls harder in a higher oxidation state, and sp carbon pulls harder than sp3 carbon.
The triangle classifies binary main-group compounds. It says little about coordination compounds and nothing at all about bond strength or reaction rate.
models.embodied_by: Nothing, and that is a fair reflection of the chemistry. No electronegativity value and no bond-type classification enters any Kerotakis solver, because thermodynamics never needs the ionic-covalent distinction: the free energy of a species does not know what kind of bond it has.

registers.lv1: In a shared pair of electrons, one atom nearly always pulls harder than the other. Pull about equally and the sharing is fair. Pull a little harder and that end goes slightly negative while the other goes slightly positive, which is why water sticks to itself so well. Pull hard enough and you do not share at all — you take, and you have made a salt. So sharing and taking are not two different things. They are the two ends of one scale, with everything real somewhere in between.
registers.lv2: Electronegativity (chi) measures an atom's pull on a bonding pair. It rises towards the top right of the periodic table: F 4.0, O 3.5, Cl 3.0, H 2.1, Na 0.9 on the Pauling scale. A difference near zero gives a nonpolar covalent bond; a moderate difference gives a polar covalent bond with partial charges; a large difference gives an ionic bond. Plot the difference against the average and you get the bond triangle (Bindungsdreieck), with metallic bonding in the low-electronegativity corner: one diagram holding all three bonding models at once.
registers.lv3: Pauling defined chi thermochemically in 1932 from the excess energy of heteronuclear bonds; Mulliken from the mean of ionisation energy and electron affinity; Allen from free-atom configuration energies. The van Arkel-Ketelaar triangle plots the difference against the mean and was made quantitative by Sproul, Jensen and Allen in the 1990s. Treat every boundary drawn on it as convention. The value of the picture is that a learner who met ionic, covalent and metallic bonding as three separate stories can now see one two-parameter family in which every real bond has all three characters in some proportion.

provenance.source: Pauling, The nature of the chemical bond, Journal of the American Chemical Society, 1932; van Arkel (1941) and Ketelaar (1947) for the triangle; quantitative versions from Sproul, Jensen and Allen in the 1990s. Editorial judgement (Kerotakis): treating the triangle as the model that supersedes the three separate bonding models, rather than as an optional extra at the end of the topic, is our ordering choice — made because the three-boxes account is the one learners most reliably over-apply

models.name: Intermolecular forces (Zwischenmolekulare Kräfte)
models.power: Separates how strong the bond inside a molecule is from how strongly molecules stick to each other, and that separation is what makes boiling points, solubility and like-dissolves-like predictable. From a structural formula alone a learner can rank substances by boiling point and say whether one will dissolve in water.
explains: boiling points rising along the alkanes, and alcohols boiling far above alkanes of the same size
water's anomalously high boiling point, and why ice floats
why oil and water do not mix
surface tension, and why water beads on a waxed car
why molecular substances melt low although their internal bonds are strong
base pairing in DNA and the folding of proteins, later on
fails_at: It ranks rather than calculates, and the ranking inverts: iodine is nonpolar and sublimes at 114 degrees, while polar HCl boils at minus 85. Dispersion forces in a large molecule beat dipole forces in a small one, and the hierarchy of adjectives cannot tell you when.
The name hydrogen bond invites the classic exam error of explaining boiling by breaking O-H bonds inside the molecule. Boiling separates molecules; every one of them leaves whole.
It cannot handle the hydrophobic effect, which is mainly entropic: oil and water separate less because oil attracts oil than because of what water has to do around it.
Quantitative prediction of boiling points and miscibility needs an activity model or an equation of state, not a list of force names.
models.embodied_by: Only its consequences, and the engine says where it stops. Hydrated ions, neutral complexes and water's own activity are all in the aqueous results, but nothing computes an intermolecular force: asked to evaporate a mixture, the bench refuses honestly and reports that co-evaporation needs vapour-liquid equilibrium, which is PLAN.md's unbuilt L3 layer.

registers.lv1: Inside a molecule the atoms are held together very tightly. But molecules also stick to each other, much more weakly, like magnets that are only mildly interested. Boiling water does not tear water molecules apart — it only pulls them away from each other, and every molecule leaves in one piece. Molecules that stick to each other more strongly need more heat before they will let go. And things dissolve in things they stick to: sugar in water, grease in petrol, never grease in water.
registers.lv2: Between molecules act, in rising strength for molecules of comparable size: London dispersion forces (always present, growing with size and surface), dipole-dipole forces (in polar molecules), and hydrogen bonds (hydrogen bound to N, O or F, meeting a lone pair). Boiling overcomes these and not the covalent bonds, which is why water boils at 100 degrees and H2S at minus 60, and why hydrogen bonds holding an open hexagonal lattice make ice less dense than water. Gleiches löst sich in Gleichem is the same idea applied to mixing.
registers.lv3: Collectively the van der Waals forces: London dispersion is an instantaneous-multipole correlation effect scaling as r to the minus sixth and growing with polarisability; Keesom and Debye terms cover dipole-dipole and dipole-induced-dipole; hydrogen bonding is partly electrostatic and partly charge transfer and is not merely a strong dipole interaction. Two cautions worth teaching: dispersion is not the weak one — it is what makes iodine a solid and HCl a gas — and the hydrophobic effect is an entropic phenomenon in the water rather than an attraction between the solutes. Quantitatively this is the domain of activity models and equations of state such as UNIFAC and PC-SAFT.

provenance.source: Standard curriculum; van der Waals (1873); London, Zeitschrift für Physik, 1930; the entropic account of the hydrophobic effect per Kauzmann and Tanford. The misconception that boiling breaks covalent bonds is documented in the bonding-misconceptions literature (e.g. Taber; Barker & Millar)

models.name: Conservation of mass (Gesetz von der Erhaltung der Masse)
models.power: Turns a reaction into an accounting problem. Once nothing can be lost, an unknown mass can be calculated instead of measured, an equation has to balance, and any experiment that seems to gain or lose mass becomes a question — where did it go? — rather than a result. It is the first law in chemistry that lets a learner predict a number.
explains: why a chemical equation must balance
why a candle burning in a sealed jar keeps its mass
why iron gains mass as it rusts and magnesium gains mass as it burns
why an open beaker of fizzing vinegar loses mass
the basis of every stoichiometric calculation
fails_at: It holds only in a closed system. In an open beaker it appears to be false, and that appearance is the most productive confusion in school chemistry, because the gas that left is invisible.

It is not exactly true. Mass and energy are equivalent, so an exothermic reaction really does lose mass — about 30 nanograms per tonne of coal burnt. Unmeasurable in chemistry, decisive in nuclear physics.
It says nothing about whether a reaction happens, how fast, or in which direction — only about the bookkeeping if it does.
models.embodied_by: Enforced rather than assumed. kerotakis-core's conservation test runs 256 randomised operator sequences and asserts that per-species mass balances to 1e-9 and that the bench's enthalpy tracks the heat budget; the Gibbs minimiser conserves elements exactly in a separate test. Charge is delegated rather than checked here: the aqueous input line ends in `pH 7 charge`, so PHREEQC balances the solution's charge and the codex says so instead of quietly implying we did it. The open-system case is modelled too — an open beaker of vinegar and baking soda fizzes most of its carbonate away and the balance shows the mass leaving.

registers.lv1: Whatever you start with you still have, even when it looks as though it has gone. Burn a candle inside a sealed jar and weigh the jar: exactly the same as before. Do it in the open and it seems to get lighter, but only because the new stuff floated off as invisible gas. Nothing in chemistry ever really disappears — it only moves, or changes its clothes.
registers.lv2: In a closed system the total mass before a reaction equals the total mass after (Lavoisier, 1789), because atoms are rearranged and never created or destroyed. That is exactly what a balanced equation asserts: the same count of each element on both sides. Apparent violations are open systems — magnesium burning gains the mass of oxygen taken from the air, and limestone in acid loses the mass of the carbon dioxide that escapes.
registers.lv3: Lavoisier's law was an experimental claim made possible by the sealed vessel and the analytical balance, and what it displaced was not a fact but a bookkeeping: phlogiston. Strictly the conserved quantity is mass-energy, and the mass defect of a chemical reaction is about one part in ten billion, which is why chemistry could be built as though mass were separately conserved. In this engine mass balance is a property test rather than a doctrine, and the balance reading less after a fizz is a computed observation rather than a lesson-writer's promise.

provenance.source: Lavoisier, Traité élémentaire de chimie (1789); mass-energy equivalence from Einstein (1905). Open-system mass loss computed by Kerotakis L2 (PHREEQC, escaping CO2 phase); conservation enforced by the proptest suite in kerotakis-core
provenance.computed_by: kerotakis-core conservation property tests; kerotakis-cea element balance

models.name: The donor-acceptor concept (Donator-Akzeptor-Prinzip)
models.power: Collapses two apparently unrelated halves of the syllabus into one idea: a proton transfer and an electron transfer are the same kind of event. Both come as a pair of half-reactions, both define conjugate pairs, and both are ordered by a strength table read the same way — so a learner who has the concept can use a redox series exactly as they use a pKa table, and predict the direction of either from one rule.
explains: acids and bases as proton donors and acceptors
oxidation and reduction as electron donation and acceptance
conjugate pairs in both families: HA/A- and Ox/Red
why oxidation never happens without reduction
half-equations, and why the electrons must cancel
why the electrochemical series and the acid-strength table are the same kind of object
fails_at: The analogy is not an identity. A hydrated proton is a real species with a concentration a meter can read; there is no corresponding free electron in solution, so the electron activity is a bookkeeping construct rather than something you can measure directly.
It gives direction, never rate. Hydrogen and oxygen sit together indefinitely although the electron transfer is overwhelmingly favourable, and the concept has nowhere to put that fact.
Real waters are usually in redox disequilibrium: different couples in the same sample imply different potentials, so a single number for the whole solution is a fiction.
It does not reach Lewis acid-base chemistry, where a pair is donated and no proton moves at all.
models.embodied_by: Half of it, and the missing half is exactly the interesting one. The aqueous solver computes proton chemistry directly — pH from charge balance, weak-acid speciation, buffers — but no electron activity or redox potential reaches a result today, so the engine currently embodies the proton wing of a concept whose whole claim is that both wings are one thing. That gap is stated here rather than papered over.

registers.lv1: An enormous number of reactions are one thing handing something over to another. Sometimes what gets handed over is a proton, a tiny positive scrap of an atom: that is an acid giving to a base. Sometimes it is an electron: that is what rusting, burning and batteries are. Either way there is always a giver and a taker, and you can never have one without the other — nobody hands something over to nobody.
registers.lv2: Two families of reaction, one pattern. Acid-base: a proton donor and a proton acceptor, forming conjugate pairs HA/A- and B/BH+. Redox: an electron donor (the reducing agent) and an electron acceptor (the oxidising agent), again in conjugate pairs Red/Ox. Both are written as two half-reactions that must add up with nothing left over, and in both the direction is read off a table of strengths — pKa for protons, standard potential for electrons.
registers.lv3: The Donator-Akzeptor-Konzept is the German curriculum's explicit unification and it is a structural insight rather than a mnemonic: both families are transfer equilibria described by an intensity variable — pH for protons, pe or Eh for electrons — and a capacity variable, the buffer intensity or the poise. Its limits are equally structural. The electron activity is formal, and natural systems are frequently in redox disequilibrium, so different couples in one water sample imply different potentials, a discrepancy documented in the groundwater literature. Lewis generalises the pattern one step further, to electron pairs, at which point complex formation joins the same family.

provenance.source: Standard German curriculum (Donator-Akzeptor-Prinzip); Brønsted and Lowry (1923) for the proton case; the pe formalism per Stumm & Morgan, Aquatic Chemistry. Redox disequilibrium in natural waters documented by Lindberg & Runnells, Science, 1984

models.name: Collision theory (Stoßmodell / Stoßtheorie)
models.power: Explains rate, which is the dimension every equilibrium model is blind to. It makes concentration, temperature, surface area and catalysis one mechanism — how many collisions, how hard, how well aimed — so a learner can predict which of two experiments fizzes faster and say why, instead of memorising four separate rules.
explains: why a reaction speeds up at higher concentration or pressure
why it roughly doubles in rate for every ten degrees
why powder reacts faster than a lump, and why flour dust can explode
why stirring helps a heterogeneous reaction
what a catalyst does
why a thermodynamically favourable reaction can simply not happen
fails_at: Its numbers are wrong. Hard-sphere collision frequency overestimates the rate of anything more complex than an atom reaction, often by orders of magnitude, and has to be rescued by an empirical steric factor the model itself cannot predict.
Molecules are not spheres and a collision is not instantaneous: there is no place in the model for orientation, vibration or a reaction path.
It cannot describe a reaction that slows as it is heated, or one that proceeds by tunnelling instead of over the barrier.
It suggests the rate law can be read off the equation. Real reaction orders are experimental facts about the mechanism and are frequently fractional.
models.embodied_by: Partly, and the boundary is sharp. `kerotakis-core/src/kinetics.rs` integrates curated rate laws with a bench clock, so three of this model's four claims are computed: concentration enters through the reaction order, temperature through the Arrhenius exponent — the rate roughly doubles per ten degrees without ever being told to, and a steeper barrier visibly breaks that rule of thumb — and a catalyst is modelled as a *lower activation energy* rather than a multiplier, which is what a catalyst is. What is not modelled is the fourth: surface area and stirring change nothing here, because the engine has no particle-size or mixing model, so the flour-dust half of this model's explanatory power is a stated hole. Orders are curated experimental facts rather than derived, and mechanisms remain PLAN.md's P5. The thermal solver's 500 K stand-down is still a placeholder for the kinetics it does not have.

registers.lv1: Nothing can react unless the pieces actually bump into each other — and a gentle bump is not enough. It has to be a hard bump, and pointing the right way. So anything that makes bumps more frequent or harder speeds the reaction up: more crowded, hotter, or ground into powder so there is more surface to bump into. That is why a lump of flour just sits there and a cloud of flour dust can blow up a mill.
registers.lv2: Particles react only when they collide, and only if the collision carries at least the activation energy and brings the right parts together.
