Rate therefore rises with concentration and pressure (more collisions per second), with temperature (a far larger fraction of collisions clears the activation energy, because of the tail of the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution) and with surface area. A catalyst opens a route with a lower activation energy, so more of the same collisions succeed.
registers.lv3: Simple collision theory gives a rate constant of the form Z times a steric factor times exp(-Ea/RT), where Z is the hard-sphere collision frequency and the exponential is the Maxwell-Boltzmann fraction above the barrier. It is semi-quantitative at best: for anything beyond atom-atom reactions the steric factor can be a hundred-thousandth and is not predicted by the theory, which is precisely the gap transition-state theory closes by replacing it with an entropy of activation. Worth saying explicitly: the rate doubles every ten degrees rule corresponds to an activation energy near 50 kJ/mol at room temperature and is a rule of thumb, not a law.

provenance.source: Standard curriculum kinetics; Trautz (1916) and W. C. M. Lewis (1918) for collision theory; Arrhenius, Zeitschrift für physikalische Chemie, 1889, for the temperature dependence

models.name: Energy profiles and activation (Energiediagramm, Aktivierungsenergie)
models.power: Puts thermodynamics and kinetics on one picture and keeps them apart: the height of the hill decides how fast, the difference between the two ends decides how far and whether heat comes out. That distinction — exothermic does not mean fast, and a catalyst changes the rate but not the position — is one learners otherwise conflate for years.
explains: exothermic and endothermic reactions as two shapes of the same diagram
why a fire needs a match although burning releases energy
what a catalyst does, and why it changes neither the products nor the heat released
the activated complex at the top of the barrier
why the reverse reaction has a different activation energy
enzyme action, later on
fails_at: The reaction coordinate is a one-dimensional cartoon of a many-dimensional energy surface. Real reactions branch, pass several saddle points, and sometimes have no barrier at all.
It draws the barrier as if height were the whole story of rate, but the tightness of the transition state matters as much: a well-ordered transition state is slow even over a low barrier.
It cannot produce a barrier height. Activation energies are measured, or computed by quantum chemistry — the diagram summarises a result, it does not predict one.
With energy on the axis it quietly implies that the heat released decides whether a reaction goes, which is false. Only the free-energy change does.
models.embodied_by: The two ends only. Kerotakis computes both endpoints exactly — the vessel's energy balance gives the heat released, and the Gibbs minimiser gives the products — and computes nothing in between. Barriers are PLAN.md's build-time L4-prime work (xtb, CREST, precomputed datasets) and are never a runtime calculation, so this diagram's middle is honestly empty.

registers.lv1: Draw the reaction as a hill. You start on one side and finish on the other. How high the hill is tells you how hard it is to get going, which is why a fire needs a match even though burning gives out heat. Where you finish tells you whether heat comes out — you ended lower down — or has to be put in. A catalyst digs a tunnel through the hill: same start, same finish, far easier journey.
registers.lv2: Plot energy against the reaction coordinate: reactants at one level, products at another, and a maximum between them, the activated complex or Übergangszustand. The climb from reactants to that maximum is the activation energy; the difference between reactants and products is the enthalpy change, negative when heat is released. The reverse reaction has to climb the activation energy plus that difference. A catalyst lowers the barrier for both directions equally, so it speeds the approach to equilibrium without moving where equilibrium lies.
registers.lv3: The diagram is a slice through a potential-energy surface along the minimum-energy path, and the maximum is a first-order saddle point with exactly one imaginary vibrational frequency — which is what a computational verification actually tests, together with an intrinsic-reaction-coordinate check. Transition-state theory writes the rate constant in terms of the free energy of activation, which is why the entropy of activation belongs on this picture even though the picture has no axis for it, and why school diagrams labelled energy should be read as free energy whenever they are used to argue about rate.

provenance.source: Standard curriculum; Eyring, Journal of Chemical Physics, 1935, and Evans & Polanyi, Transactions of the Faraday Society, 1935, for transition-state theory

models.name: Chemical equilibrium (Chemisches Gleichgewicht)
models.power: Replaces reactions go to completion with reactions go to a position, and gives that position a number. With an equilibrium constant a learner can predict how far a reaction gets, calculate what is left over, and grasp that a reaction can be running fast in both directions while nothing appears to change. Weak acids, buffers, solubility products and industrial yield then stop being four topics and become one.
explains: reversible reactions, and why they stop short
that equilibrium is dynamic: labelled atoms keep swapping sides after the amounts stop changing
why a weak acid only partly dissociates
solubility limits and the solubility product
how a buffer works
why an industrial process never reaches its paper yield
fails_at: It says nothing about how long. A reaction with an enormous equilibrium constant that takes a geological age is described perfectly by the model and completely misunderstood by the learner who thinks it goes.

Concentration is the wrong variable outside dilute solution: the constant is constant in activities, and in brine that correction is a factor rather than a percentage. Kerotakis can show this rather than assert it — asked the same brine question, three databases return three different amounts of undissolved salt, each labelled with the activity model that produced it.
The equilibrium constant is not constant when the temperature changes, which makes it the one constant in school chemistry that misleads by its own name.
Many real systems are not at equilibrium and stay that way. Living things most of all.
models.embodied_by: Directly, and in an unusual way: the engine never simulates a reaction proceeding. PHREEQC solves for the equilibrium distribution of every species at once, so the codex's weak-acid pH of 2.88 and its buffer behaviour emerge from the database's own equilibria instead of from a formula we applied — and the constants themselves are never printed, only their consequences. The Gibbs minimiser does the same job for gases and condensed phases by minimising the total free energy under element constraints.

registers.lv1: Some reactions never finish. They run forwards and backwards at the same time, and after a while both directions go at exactly the same speed — so the amounts stop changing even though nothing has stopped. It looks like the end, but it is more like a busy escalator with as many people walking up as down. How far a reaction gets before that happens is different for every reaction.
registers.lv2: A reversible reaction reaches a dynamic equilibrium: forward and reverse rates become equal, so concentrations become constant — constant, not equal. The law of mass action gives an equilibrium constant K as the ratio of product to reactant concentrations, each raised to its coefficient, fixed at a given temperature. K much greater than one means products dominate; much less than one means reactants do. Special cases carry their own names: Ka for weak acids, Kw for water, Ksp for sparingly soluble salts.
registers.lv3: Thermodynamically K is not an empirical summary but a consequence — the standard free-energy change in another currency — and its temperature dependence follows the van 't Hoff equation. Written properly K is a ratio of activities, and in Kerotakis that stops being a footnote: the engine computes activities alongside molalities, so the conditional pKa2 of phosphate reads about 6.65 at an ionic strength near 0.25 where the textbook table says 7.2. The textbook constant and the pH meter genuinely disagree, and the model says which is which. Equilibrium is also a canonical threshold concept — transformative, integrative, irreversible and demonstrably troublesome — with the two persistent misconceptions being that the rates stop and that the concentrations become equal.

provenance.source: Guldberg & Waage (1864) for the law of mass action; van 't Hoff (1884). Equilibrium misconceptions documented by Hackling & Garnett, European Journal of Science Education, 1985. Editorial judgement (Kerotakis): naming equilibrium a threshold concept in the Meyer-Land sense, and therefore expecting it to be troublesome rather than treating difficulty as failure, is our framing, informed by Meyer & Land (2003)
provenance.computed_by: Kerotakis L2 (PHREEQC) for the aqueous numbers; kerotakis-cea for gas and condensed phases

models.name: Le Chatelier's principle (Prinzip vom kleinsten Zwang)
models.power: Gives a direction of change with no calculation at all. Change a concentration, a pressure or a temperature and the principle tells you which way the yield moves — enough to explain the Haber process, why a fizzy drink goes flat, and why an industrial plant runs at conditions that look like a compromise, because they are one.
explains: shifting the position by adding or removing a substance
pressure changing the position when the two sides have different gas mole numbers
heating favouring the endothermic direction
why a catalyst shifts nothing
the common-ion effect
the conditions chosen for the Haber-Bosch process
fails_at: It is a heuristic and it can be led into a wrong answer. Add more nitrogen to an equilibrated ammonia synthesis at constant temperature and pressure, once nitrogen is already in excess, and the mole fraction of ammonia falls — the system opposes the change and the yield still goes down.
Adding an inert gas at constant volume changes nothing, although increasing the pressure sounds as though it should. The principle's own words mislead unless you already know the answer.
It gives a direction and never a magnitude, and the shift is often negligible.
The word Zwang invites teleology. Learners describe the system as wanting to oppose the change, a misconception the phrasing itself plants.
models.embodied_by: Never applied — always checked. The bench discards a vessel's characterisation the moment anything touches it and re-solves the whole equilibrium, so a shift is something the learner causes and the solver discovers: add a common ion, let CO2 escape from an open vessel, or warm the beaker, and the new position is computed from scratch. Le Chatelier is then a prediction to be tested against that result rather than a rule the engine obeys.

registers.lv1: Disturb a reaction that has settled down and it shuffles to undo part of what you did. Take something away and it makes more of it. Squeeze a gas mixture and it moves to whichever side takes up less room. Heat it and it moves the way that soaks heat up. It never undoes your change completely — it only pushes back a bit.
registers.lv2: Prinzip vom kleinsten Zwang: a system at equilibrium subjected to a constraint responds so as to reduce that constraint. More reactant shifts the position towards products; higher pressure shifts it towards the side with fewer gas molecules; higher temperature favours the endothermic direction. A catalyst changes neither the position nor K. Haber-Bosch is the classic compromise — high pressure helps the yield, low temperature would help it too but destroys the rate, so the plant runs hot with a catalyst, against the principle's advice.
registers.lv3: The rigorous statement is thermodynamic: at constant temperature and pressure a system moves so as to lower its Gibbs energy, and the direction after any perturbation follows from comparing the reaction quotient with the equilibrium constant. The qualitative form has genuine counterexamples — adding a reactant already in excess can lower the product mole fraction at constant pressure, and adding an inert gas at constant volume does nothing — which is why it is best treated as a heuristic with a stated domain. Teaching it together with its counterexample is the point: it is the smallest clear case of a rule that works right up until you can say when it does not.

provenance.source: Le Chatelier (1884) and Braun (1887); the reaction-quotient formulation and the counterexamples are standard in the physical-chemistry education literature (recurring subject of Journal of Chemical Education articles on the principle's limitations). Editorial judgement (Kerotakis): presenting the principle together with its counterexample rather than as a rule is our choice

models.name: Amount of substance - the mole (Stoffmenge, das Mol)
models.power: Lets you turn a mass you can weigh into a number of particles you cannot see, which is what makes any quantitative prediction possible at all. Without it a balanced equation is a sentence about atoms and a balance is a device for measuring grams, and the two never meet.
explains: converting between mass and number of particles
why equations balance in moles and not in grams
molar mass, and why it is numerically the relative atomic mass
the molar volume of a gas
concentration, limiting reagent, yield and titration, all of which are built on it
fails_at: It is not a model of anything physical. It is a unit — a chosen counting number — which is exactly why it is hard: there is nothing to picture, and a mole of something has no size, colour or feel.

Nothing in the concept records which particles you counted. A mole of water is that many molecules but three times as many atoms, and a mole of oxygen is ambiguous until somebody says O or O2. This is the single commonest source of factor-of-two errors.
The molar volume of 22.4 litres holds for an ideal gas at zero degrees and standard pressure only. Treating it as a property of gases is a routine mistake.

It hides a change of definition. Since 2019 the mole is defined by fixing Avogadro's number, not by twelve grams of carbon-12, so molar mass is now a measured quantity with an uncertainty rather than an exact one.
models.embodied_by: The bench's native unit. Every vessel holds moles: writing `add v1 NaCl 2g` converts through the registry's molar mass at the door, and everything downstream — the solvers, the balance, the conservation tests — works in amount of substance. The learner's first hard conversion is the engine's boundary condition, and the atomic weights it uses carry their own provenance (IUPAC/CIAAW 2021).

registers.lv1: Atoms are far too small to count one at a time, so chemists count them by weighing — the way you buy rice by the kilo instead of grain by grain, or eggs by the dozen instead of one by one. A mole is just a very large dozen: it is how many pieces you get in a certain weight of a substance, and it is the same number of pieces for every substance. That is the whole trick. Weigh grams, know how many pieces.
registers.lv2: The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance: one mole contains 6.02214076 times ten to the twenty-third specified entities. The molar mass in grams per mole is numerically the relative atomic or molecular mass, so dividing a mass by a molar mass converts something weighable into something countable. The coefficients in an equation are ratios of moles, which is why 24 g of magnesium needs 16 g of oxygen rather than an equal mass.
registers.lv3: Since the 2019 SI revision the mole is defined by fixing the Avogadro constant exactly, which decoupled it from the kilogram and from carbon-12; the molar mass of carbon-12 is now 12 g/mol only within a small measured uncertainty. Pedagogically it is the textbook threshold concept: transformative, since nothing quantitative is possible before it and everything is after; integrative, since it binds formula, equation, mass and volume; irreversible; and troublesome, in that learners reliably execute the arithmetic while holding no coherent idea of what a mole is, treating it variously as a mass, a volume or a number of grams. The countermeasure this codex uses is to make the calculation load-bearing: the number you derive is the number the beaker will show.

provenance.source: SI Brochure, 9th edition (BIPM, 2019); atomic weights from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 as recorded in the Kerotakis species registry. Learner difficulties with the mole documented by Novick & Menis, Journal of Chemical Education, 1976, and Staver & Lumpe, Journal of Research in Science Teaching, 1995. Editorial judgement (Kerotakis): treating the mole as a threshold concept in the Meyer-Land sense — and so expecting difficulty rather than reading it as failure — is our framing, informed by Meyer & Land (2003)

models.name: Stoichiometry (Stöchiometrie)
models.power: Makes an equation predictive in grams. Given what you put in, it tells you how much you can get out, which reagent runs out first, and how good your experiment was — before you do it. This is the point where chemistry becomes an engineering discipline rather than a description.
explains: mole ratios read straight off the coefficients
limiting and excess reagent
theoretical yield, actual yield and percentage yield
atom economy
titration calculations
empirical formula from combustion analysis
fails_at: It assumes the equation you wrote is the reaction that happened. Side reactions, incomplete conversion and impurities are invisible to it, which is why the yield is never 100 per cent and the arithmetic never warns you.
It assumes the reaction runs to completion, so the theoretical yield of an equilibrium process is not merely unachieved but unachievable.
It is arithmetic, not chemistry. It will happily compute the yield of a reaction that does not occur.
models.embodied_by: Not applied — checked. The solvers compute a final composition from thermodynamics, so the stoichiometric answer is what the learner predicts and the engine then confirms or contradicts. Burning a magnesium ribbon leaves more oxide than the ribbon weighed, and the extra mass came from air that nobody weighed in — a result that is computed here rather than told.

registers.lv1: A recipe says two eggs and 100 g of flour make eight pancakes. Chemistry works the same way: the equation is the recipe, so once you have it you can work out exactly how much you need and exactly how much you will get. And if you only have one egg it does not matter how much flour is in the cupboard — you get four pancakes. Whatever runs out first decides everything.
registers.lv2: The coefficients of a balanced equation are mole ratios, so the amount of any substance follows from the amount of any other. The limiting reagent is the one with the smallest amount divided by its coefficient; everything else is in excess. Percentage yield is the actual divided by the theoretical yield; atom economy is the mass of the desired product as a fraction of the total mass of products. They are two different questions about the same reaction, and a reaction can score well on one and badly on the other.
registers.lv3: Stoichiometry is linear algebra over the element-composition matrix: balancing an equation is finding a null-space vector, and the number of independent reactions in a mixture is that matrix's rank deficiency. The educational risk here is documented rather than hypothetical — proportional-reasoning algorithms can be executed correctly by learners who cannot say what a limiting reagent is, so success on the calculation is weak evidence of understanding. Predict-observe-explain is this codex's countermeasure: commit to the number first, then let the solver settle it.

provenance.source: Standard curriculum. The gap between algorithmic success and conceptual understanding in stoichiometry documented by Nurrenbern & Pickering, Journal of Chemical Education, 1987, and Sawrey, Journal of Chemical Education, 1990; predict-observe-explain from White & Gunstone, Probing Understanding (1992)

models.name: Concentration (Konzentration)
models.power: Makes how much independent of how much you took. Concentration is intensive, so it can be compared between a test tube and a lake, carried through a dilution, and put straight into an equilibrium expression or a rate law. It is also what turns a titration from a colour change into a measurement.
explains: amount concentration as amount divided by volume
dilution, and why the amount of solute does not change
titration, and how an unknown concentration is obtained from a known one
pH as a concentration on a logarithmic scale
why a drop of bleach and a bottle of it are different hazards
fails_at: Molar concentration depends on temperature, because the volume does. Molality does not, which is why thermodynamic work — and every number this engine computes — is per kilogram of water rather than per litre of solution, and why the two are not interchangeable once a solution is concentrated.

Concentration is not what an equilibrium responds to. Activity is. In dilute solution they nearly coincide; at an ionic strength of 0.1 mol/kgw the activity coefficient of the silver ion is already about 0.78, and in brine the correction is a factor, not a percentage.
It says nothing about which species are present. 0.1 mol/L phosphoric acid is a recipe, not a description: the solution actually holds four phosphate species in a pH-dependent mixture.
Volumes do not add exactly, so a dilution calculation is an approximation — mixing 50 mL of ethanol with 50 mL of water gives about 96 mL.
models.embodied_by: The engine works in molality per kilogram of water and reports each species' activity beside its molality, so the difference between the two is visible rather than asserted — the activity coefficient is a ratio the learner can read off. Which activity model produced it is stated with the answer, together with its range: the WATEQ Debye-Hückel extension to about I = 1 mol/kgw, the Davies equation to about 0.5, the Pitzer ion-interaction model beyond.

registers.lv1: It is not enough to know what is in the water — you need to know how crowded it is. One spoon of sugar in a cup is sweet; the same spoon in a bathtub is nothing at all. Concentration is that crowding, and it decides whether something tastes strong, whether it works, and whether it is dangerous.
registers.lv2: Amount concentration is amount of substance divided by volume of solution, in mol/L. Adding solvent does not change the amount of solute, which gives the dilution relation: the product of concentration and volume is the same before and after. Titration uses this directly — at the equivalence point the amounts of acid and base are equal, so the unknown concentration follows from the standard's concentration and the two volumes.
registers.lv3: Distinguish three quantities that school chemistry runs together: concentration (per litre of solution, temperature-dependent), molality (per kilogram of solvent, temperature-independent, the thermodynamic choice) and activity, which is what equilibrium constants and electrode potentials actually contain. The activity coefficient comes from a model with a stated validity range, and Kerotakis surfaces both the number and the model — put the same brine question to three databases and they disagree about how much salt stays undissolved, each answer labelled with the activity model behind it. That disagreement is not a defect to be hidden; it is a model boundary made visible by driving the model past it.

provenance.source: Standard curriculum; activity models and their validity ranges declared by the PHREEQC databases themselves (USGS, public domain), read out of the database files rather than assumed
provenance.licence: PHREEQC databases: USGS User Rights Notice (public-domain-like, attribution)
provenance.computed_by: Kerotakis L2 (PHREEQC via IPhreeqc)

models.name: Arrhenius acid-base model (Arrhenius-Definition)
models.power: The first definition that makes acid a statement about composition rather than about taste. It predicts that every acid neutralises every base to give a salt and water, explains why acid and alkali solutions conduct, and reduces hundreds of neutralisations to a single ionic equation.
explains: acids as substances that give H+ in water, bases as substances that give OH-
neutralisation as one reaction: H+ plus OH- gives water
why acid and alkali solutions conduct electricity
salt formation as what is left over
the pH scale in water
why a strong acid conducts better than a weak one at the same concentration
fails_at: It cannot explain why ammonia is a base. There is no hydroxide anywhere in NH3, and its solution is alkaline anyway. That single fact is what forced the next model.
It is confined to water. Hydrogen chloride dissolved in benzene, or acid-base chemistry in liquid ammonia, is invisible to it.
The bare proton it invokes does not exist in solution; at minimum it is hydrated as H3O+.
It defines an acid by what the substance contains rather than by what happens in the reaction, so it cannot say that a species acts as an acid in one reaction and a base in another.
models.embodied_by: Faithfully, and that is a limitation worth showing. PHREEQC's model is aqueous, so all of the engine's acid-base chemistry lives inside Arrhenius's domain even where the codex speaks Brønsted's language. An acid in a non-aqueous solvent is not merely unimplemented here; it is outside what the solver can express.

registers.lv1: Some liquids taste sour and fizz on metals; others feel slippery and soapy. The sour ones put a special positive scrap into the water, and the soapy ones put in a scrap that cancels it exactly. Mix the right amounts and both disappear, leaving salty water. That is what neutral means — and in a lab you never taste anything to find out.
registers.lv2: Arrhenius (1887): an acid dissociates in water to give H+, a base to give OH-. Hydrochloric acid gives H+ and Cl-; sodium hydroxide gives Na+ and OH-. Every neutralisation is then the same reaction, H+ plus OH- to water, with the remaining ions making up a salt. Acid strength is the extent of that dissociation, which is why hydrochloric acid conducts far better than acetic acid at equal concentration.
registers.lv3: Arrhenius's theory of electrolytic dissociation was radical enough in 1887 to nearly cost him his doctorate and won him the Nobel Prize in 1903; its strength was quantitative, since conductivity data and colligative anomalies both fell out of the same idea. Its boundary is structural rather than accidental: by defining acidity as a property of a substance dissolved in water, it has no way to describe a proton transfer, which is why ammonia's basicity has no explanation inside it and why what follows is a change of subject rather than an extension.

provenance.source: Arrhenius, Zeitschrift für physikalische Chemie, 1887 (Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 1903)

models.name: Brønsted-Lowry model (Brønsted-Lowry, Protonenübergang)
models.power: Redefines acid and base as roles in a reaction rather than properties of substances, and with that one move explains ammonia, buffers, why salt solutions can be acidic or basic, water's ability to act as both, and acid-base chemistry outside water entirely. It also makes acid strength comparative and tabulated: conjugate pairs order themselves, and the transfer runs from the stronger acid to the stronger base.
explains: ammonia as a base with no hydroxide in it
conjugate acid-base pairs
amphoteric species such as water and hydrogencarbonate
why sodium acetate solution is basic and ammonium chloride solution acidic
buffers, and why they resist added acid
the shape of a titration curve
fails_at: There has to be a proton. It has nothing to say about boron trifluoride meeting ammonia, about metal-ion catalysis, or about why aluminium chloride is called an acid at all.
Its strength scale is bound to the solvent. In water every acid stronger than H3O+ looks equally strong, so hydrochloric, hydrobromic and perchloric acid cannot be told apart in water at all.
It gives position and direction but no rate, and proton transfers are not always fast — carbon acids can be extremely slow.
A pKa is not a constant of nature. It shifts with ionic strength, which is why a textbook table and a real pH meter disagree.
models.embodied_by: This is the model the aqueous solver actually runs on. PHREEQC's databases are built from proton-transfer equilibria with their own log K values, so the codex's weak-acid pH, its buffer and its titration curve are Brønsted equilibria being solved rather than formulae being applied — including the parts that embarrass the textbook, such as phosphate's conditional pKa2 reading about 6.65 at working ionic strength instead of 7.2.

registers.lv1: Forget sour and soapy. An acid is anything that hands over a proton — one tiny positive particle — and a base is anything that takes one. So being an acid is not something a substance is, it is something it does, and with a different partner the same substance can do the opposite. Water does both: it gives protons to ammonia and takes them from vinegar.
registers.lv2: Brønsted and Lowry (1923): an acid is a proton donor, a base a proton acceptor, and every acid-base reaction is a proton transfer between two conjugate pairs. Ammonia plus water gives ammonium plus hydroxide, with no hydroxide needed in the ammonia. Water is amphoteric. Ka, and its negative logarithm pKa, measures how far the transfer to water goes, so the direction of any proton transfer can be read straight off a pKa table: from the stronger acid to the stronger base.
registers.lv3: This is the German curriculum's Protonenübergang and, with redox, the standard instance of the donor-acceptor pattern. Its structural advance is that acidity becomes a property of a couple rather than of a compound, which is what lets conjugate pairs, buffers and the levelling effect all be stated in one language. Two refinements belong at this level: the proton in water is not free, and the hydronium formulation is itself a simplification of Eigen and Zundel structures; and tabulated Ka values are thermodynamic constants at infinite dilution that must be converted to conditional constants at real ionic strength before they will match an instrument.

provenance.source: Brønsted, Recueil des Travaux Chimiques des Pays-Bas, 1923, and Lowry, 1923, independently; conditional constants and ionic-strength corrections per Stumm & Morgan, Aquatic Chemistry
provenance.computed_by: Kerotakis L2 (PHREEQC, minteq.v4 for the phosphate case)

models.name: Lewis acid-base model (Lewis-Säure-Base-Konzept)
models.power: Generalises acidity from gives a proton to accepts an electron pair, which brings metal ions, boron trifluoride, catalysis, complex formation and much of organic mechanism under one heading. It also joins the acid-base story to the donor-acceptor story and to curly arrows: a nucleophile is a Lewis base and an electrophile a Lewis acid.
explains: the adduct of boron trifluoride and ammonia, an acid-base reaction with no proton in it
why solutions of aluminium and iron(III) salts are acidic
complex formation between a metal ion and its ligands
Friedel-Crafts catalysis
nucleophile and electrophile as one idea rather than two vocabularies
the proton as a special case: an acceptor with no electrons of its own
fails_at: There is no single strength scale. Lewis acid strength depends on which base you measure it against, which is why the hard-and-soft classification had to be invented and why it stays qualitative.
It is so general that it stops discriminating: under this definition nearly every reaction is an acid-base reaction, which is true and rarely useful.
It gives nothing quantitative for aqueous acidity, so the proton chemistry a school course actually needs still runs on Brønsted.
models.embodied_by: Partly, and by the back door. The databases carry metal-complexation equilibria — the neutral AgCl(aq) complex and the hydrolysis of metal aquo ions are Lewis acid-base chemistry — but the solver has no notion of a Lewis acid. It has log K values for complexes. The concept explains the numbers; it does not produce them.

registers.lv1: The deepest version of acid has nothing to do with protons at all. Some atoms have a spare pair of electrons to offer and some have an empty space that would fit one. Put them together and the pair moves in, making a bond out of one partner's electrons alone. A proton is simply the smallest thing there is with an empty space — so the older rules were a special case of this one all along.
registers.lv2: Lewis (1923): an acid accepts an electron pair, a base donates one, and the result is a coordinate or dative bond. Boron trifluoride plus ammonia is an acid-base reaction with no proton anywhere. H+ fits the definition as the limiting case. It also explains why solutions of Al3+ and Fe3+ are acidic — the metal ion is a Lewis acid polarising its water ligands until one of them releases a proton — and why complex formation, catalysis and nucleophilic attack are all the same kind of event.
registers.lv3: Lewis subsumes Brønsted, which subsumes Arrhenius; Usanovich's broader definition subsumes Lewis in turn and is not used, because it dissolves the distinction entirely. The practical weakness is the absence of a universal scale: Lewis acidity is base-dependent, addressed empirically by Pearson's hard-and-soft principle and by Drago-Wayland parameters rather than by one number. This is also the clearest case in the curriculum of a model succession that is a generalisation rather than a correction — Arrhenius is not wrong within water, it is a special case — and that difference is worth naming aloud, because learners otherwise infer that each earlier model was simply mistaken.

provenance.source: Lewis, Valence and the Structure of Atoms and Molecules (1923); Pearson, Hard and soft acids and bases, Journal of the American Chemical Society, 1963. Editorial judgement (Kerotakis): flagging Arrhenius to Brønsted to Lewis as generalisation rather than correction is our emphasis, chosen because the progression is otherwise read as three successive refutations

models.name: Enthalpy (Enthalpie, Reaktionsenthalpie)
models.power: Puts a number on it got hot. Energy becomes a bookkeeping quantity like mass: tabulated per substance, additive along any route, and therefore predictable for reactions nobody has ever measured. It also says why making bonds releases energy and breaking them costs it, so a reaction's heat can be estimated from a table.
explains: exothermic and endothermic reactions
why some things warm the beaker on dissolving and others chill it
calorimetry, and how a heat of reaction is measured
Hess's law: the same heat by any route
standard formation enthalpies, and reaction enthalpies computed from them
the energy content of fuels and of food
fails_at: It does not predict whether a reaction happens, although it feels as though it should. Ammonium nitrate dissolving is strongly endothermic and happens by itself; ice above zero absorbs heat and melts anyway. Systems tend towards lower energy is the most common false generalisation in school chemistry.
Bond-enthalpy estimates are averages taken across many different molecules, so they can be tens of kilojoules per mole out, and they apply to gases rather than to liquids or solids.
It is defined at constant pressure and says nothing about how the energy is distributed, or about its own temperature dependence, until heat capacities are brought in.
models.embodied_by: Directly, and with its own stated limits. Each vessel carries an energy balance: enthalpy is tracked as the sum of amount times heat capacity above 298.15 K, mixing solves for a common temperature rather than assuming one, and curated dissolution enthalpies move the thermometer — calcium chloride is a hot pack, potassium chloride a cold one. Two honest gaps: heat capacities are treated as temperature-independent in the aqueous path, and curated reactions carry no reaction enthalpy yet, so no heat effect is applied where none is known. The thermal solver is separate and better founded — NASA-9 polynomials give H(T) per species, and an adiabatic vessel is solved enthalpy-conserving rather than by dividing a reaction enthalpy by a heat capacity.

registers.lv1: Reactions do not only change what things are, they change how hot things are. Some give heat out, so the beaker warms up: burning, and the packs you snap to warm your hands. Some take heat in, so the beaker goes cold enough to freeze a puddle to the bench — that is what a cold pack is. Pulling things apart always costs energy and joining them up always gives energy back, and whichever is bigger decides whether it warms or cools.
registers.lv2: The enthalpy change is the heat exchanged at constant pressure: negative when heat is released, positive when it is absorbed. It is a state function, so Hess's law lets it be added along any route, and standard formation enthalpies let any reaction's value be found as products minus reactants. Estimated from bonds, it is the energy of the bonds broken minus the energy of the bonds formed.
registers.lv3: Enthalpy is internal energy plus pressure times volume, and its change equals the heat at constant pressure for a closed system doing only expansion work. Hess's law is a consequence of its being a state function, and the whole tabulated apparatus of thermochemistry rests on that one property. Its temperature dependence follows from the difference in heat capacities, which is exactly what the NASA-9 polynomial form encodes: seven coefficients per temperature interval yielding heat capacity, enthalpy and entropy for a species. The decisive teaching point here is negative — enthalpy is not the criterion for spontaneity, and treating it as one is a persistent documented misconception that the next two models exist to correct.

provenance.source: Standard thermodynamics; Hess's law (1840). The misconception that exothermicity determines spontaneity documented by Boo, Journal of Research in Science Teaching, 1998, and Sözbilir & Bennett, Journal of Chemical Education, 2007
provenance.computed_by: kerotakis-core's vessel energy balance; kerotakis-cea for H(T) from NASA-9 coefficients

models.name: Entropy (Entropie)
models.power: Supplies the second reason things happen. Once you can count how many ways a state can be arranged, you can predict that gases mix and never unmix, that some solids dissolve even though it costs energy, and that heat flows one way only — none of which enthalpy can give you. It turns why does anything happen by itself into a question with an answer.
explains: why mixing is irreversible: milk never comes back out of the coffee
why a salt can dissolve while making the beaker cold
why a gas expands into a vacuum with no push
why heat flows from hot to cold and never back
why a reaction that makes a gas has a strongly positive entropy change
why a perfect crystal is the low-entropy case
fails_at: Entropy is disorder is the metaphor that does most of the damage. Disorder is undefined, and the cases that matter look like the metaphor's opposite: oil separating from water and a supercooled liquid freezing both look tidier and are both entropy-driven overall.

The system's entropy alone predicts nothing. Water freezing lowers it and is spontaneous below zero, because the surroundings gain more than the system loses — and counting the surroundings is exactly the step learners skip.
It is statistical, so it is a near-certainty rather than a law: small systems fluctuate the wrong way, and the second law is a statement about overwhelming probability.
It gives no rate at all. Diamond turning into graphite raises the entropy of the universe and takes geological time.
models.embodied_by: Computed and deliberately not displayed. NASA-9 coefficients give an entropy for every species at every temperature, and it drives the Gibbs minimiser — but no result field in Kerotakis carries an entropy, so what a learner sees is the consequence rather than the quantity. The consequence is real enough: at 3000 K the combustion products visibly break up into CO, OH and H, which is entropy outbidding bond energy, computed rather than asserted.

registers.lv1: There are far more ways for things to end up mixed than tidy, so mixing happens by itself and unmixing never does. Stir milk into coffee and it will not come back out however long you keep stirring. Heat spreads out for the same reason: there are more ways to share the jiggling around than to keep it all in one corner. This is why things happen on their own even when no energy is released.
registers.lv2: Entropy counts the microscopic arrangements a state can be made of. It rises when gases form, when solids dissolve, and whenever anything mixes. The second law says the entropy of the universe never decreases in a spontaneous process, which means the system's change plus the surroundings' change must be positive. That is how an endothermic dissolution can still happen by itself: the system gains more entropy than the surroundings lose in giving up the heat.
registers.lv3: Boltzmann's statistical definition and Clausius's thermodynamic one are the two faces of the same quantity, and the third law fixes the zero — which is why absolute entropies are tabulated where enthalpies must be referred to formation. Teach it as the spreading of energy over accessible states rather than as disorder: the disorder metaphor is criticised in the chemistry-education literature precisely because it mispredicts the interesting cases, from protein folding to hydrophobic aggregation to crystallisation. The system-only shortcut everyone actually uses is the Gibbs energy, which is the total entropy change wearing different clothes.

provenance.source: Clausius (1865); Boltzmann (1877). The case against teaching entropy as disorder is made by Lambert, Journal of Chemical Education, 2002; student difficulties documented by Sözbilir & Bennett, Journal of Chemical Education, 2007
provenance.computed_by: kerotakis-cea (S(T) from NASA-9 coefficients, used internally by the Gibbs minimiser)

models.name: Gibbs free energy (Gibbs-Energie, freie Enthalpie)
models.power: The single criterion for whether a reaction can happen at all. It folds enthalpy and entropy into one number whose sign answers the question every earlier model dodged, tells you the temperature at which the answer flips, and — through its relation to the equilibrium constant — makes does it go and how far does it go the same calculation. It is the top of the school chemistry model hierarchy.
explains: why some reactions are spontaneous and others are not
why endothermic reactions can happen by themselves
why limestone decomposes in a kiln and not in a beaker
why some reactions reverse on heating
the link between the free-energy change and the equilibrium constant
cell voltages, and why a battery has the voltage it has
fails_at: Spontaneous means possible, not actual. Diamond, petrol in air and a stick of dynamite are all thermodynamically doomed and are all sitting still. The free energy says nothing about rate, and every kinetics model exists in the gap it leaves.
It is the criterion at constant temperature and pressure only. At constant volume the right quantity is the Helmholtz energy, and far from equilibrium neither applies.

The standard free-energy change tells you where equilibrium lies, not which way your actual mixture will move. That needs the reaction quotient compared with the constant, and the two are confused constantly.
Tabulated values assume ideal behaviour: in real solutions activity coefficients matter, and in melts and solid solutions the mixing terms defeat simple tables.
models.embodied_by: This is the engine's floor. kerotakis-cea minimises the mixture's total Gibbs energy directly — the Gordon and McBride formulation, one Lagrange multiplier per element, a damped Newton iteration on the logarithms of the amounts, condensed phases admitted or dropped by comparing chemical potentials — so is this possible is not looked up anywhere. It is the answer to an optimisation. Chalk is stable at 800 K and fully calcined by 1400 K with the decomposition temperature computed, and methane in air reaches an adiabatic flame temperature near 2225 K, found by bisecting on enthalpy, because that is where the free energy is lowest.

registers.lv1: Whether something happens by itself is a contest between two things: does it give out heat, and does it end up more spread about. If both say yes it happens. If both say no it never does. If they disagree, the temperature is the referee — which is why water freezes by itself when it is cold and not when it is warm, and why chalk turns to quicklime only once the kiln is hot enough. But can happen is not will happen soon: a diamond ought to turn into pencil lead, and does not, because nothing pushes it over the hill.
registers.lv2: The Gibbs energy change is the enthalpy change minus the temperature times the entropy change. Negative means the reaction is spontaneous as written, positive means the reverse is, zero means equilibrium. Because the entropy term is multiplied by temperature, a reaction that absorbs heat but increases entropy becomes spontaneous above a switch-over temperature — the enthalpy change divided by the entropy change — which is exactly why limestone decomposes in a kiln and not in a beaker. At equilibrium the standard free-energy change is fixed by the equilibrium constant, so free energy and K are one statement in two notations.
registers.lv3: The Gibbs energy is enthalpy minus temperature times entropy, and at constant temperature and pressure a spontaneous change lowers it — which is the second law rewritten in variables belonging to the system alone. Equilibrium is then the minimum of G subject to element-balance constraints, and that is a computable statement rather than a rhetorical one: it is literally what a Gibbs minimiser does, and what PHREEQC's mass-action formulation is equivalent to. Two boundaries this codex insists on. Spontaneity is not rate, which is why the thermal solver stands down below 500 K instead of oxidising every metal on the bench. And the standard state is a choice, so the standard free-energy change and the actual one answer different questions.

provenance.source: Gibbs, On the equilibrium of heterogeneous substances, Transactions of the Connecticut Academy, 1876-78; minimiser formulation from Gordon & McBride, NASA RP-1311; thermodynamic data from NASA CEA thermo.inp
provenance.licence: NASA CEA data: Apache-2.0; NASA RP-1311: US Government work
provenance.computed_by: kerotakis-cea (Gibbs minimisation over NASA-9 polynomials)

models.name: Thermodynamic versus kinetic control
models.power: Separates two questions that beginners hear as one: which product is the most stable, and which product you actually get. Once they come apart, a whole class of otherwise baffling observations becomes predictable — why the blue precipitate is not the black one, why diamond does not turn into graphite on the shelf, why the shelf itself is not on fire. It also tells you what to do about it: if the barrier is what stands in the way, heat it, and the stable product appears.
explains: why adding lye to copper sulfate gives pale blue Cu(OH)2 and not black CuO, even though CuO is the more stable solid
why warming that suspension turns it black — the classic demonstration
why diamond, graphite and every metastable mineral persist indefinitely
why a Gibbs-minimising calculation can be right about the destination and wrong about the beaker
Ostwald's rule of stages: the phase that appears first is often the least stable one available, because it nucleates fastest
why magnesium ribbon sits in air until you light it
fails_at: It says which product is kinetically preferred only after you already know the barriers. On its own it predicts nothing quantitative — it is a frame for two other models, not a third model that replaces them.
It gives no timescale. "Metastable" covers both a precipitate that converts in a minute of warming and a diamond that outlasts the solar system, and nothing in the idea distinguishes them.
Nucleation, not just the activation barrier, decides which solid appears first, and surface energy and supersaturation belong to a theory this framing does not contain.

Applied carelessly it becomes unfalsifiable: any disagreement between calculation and observation can be waved away as kinetics. It is only worth anything when the barrier is named and the conditions that overcome it are stated.
models.embodied_by: Directly, and with the seam visible. The aqueous engine minimises free energy, so left alone it returns tenorite (CuO) — more stable than Cu(OH)2 by 1.03 log units in minteq.v4. A beaker gives the blue hydroxide. The registry therefore carries `forms_only_above_k` on copper(II) oxide: below 340 K the phase is withheld from the solver, above it the engine is free to find it, and `heat v1 20kJ` really does turn the blue solid black at 77 C. The threshold is curated and says so — a stated stand-in for a rate we do not model, not a measurement. The same admission appears twice more in the engine: the thermal solver stands down below 500 K rather than oxidising every metal on the bench, and the aqueous solver now reports when a solution is supersaturated against a phase it is holding back, so the kinetic claim is visible rather than silent.

registers.lv1: Chemistry has a favourite answer and a fast answer, and they are not always the same one. Mix the blue copper liquid with drain cleaner and you get a pale blue jelly. That jelly is not what the chemistry would settle on if it had forever — the black powder is — but the jelly forms quickly and then just sits there, because turning into the black powder is hard work. Warm it up and it turns black in front of you. Most of the world is like this: your chair is not the most stable thing its atoms could be, it is just stuck.
registers.lv2: Two different questions: which product has the lowest free energy (thermodynamic control) and which product forms fastest (kinetic control). At low temperature the fastest-forming product wins and can persist indefinitely, because the barrier to rearranging into the stable one is far larger than the available thermal energy. Raise the temperature and the barrier becomes surmountable, so the stable product takes over. Cu(OH)2 versus CuO is the school case; Ostwald's rule of stages generalises it, saying that a crystallising system tends to pass through the least stable form first because that is the one that nucleates most easily.
registers.lv3: The distinction is between a state function and a rate. Equilibrium thermodynamics fixes the destination and is silent on the path, so a free-energy minimisation is answering a question the beaker may not be asking. Where barriers greatly exceed RT the observed composition is set by the relative heights of transition states, and Curtin-Hammett conditions describe when product ratios follow those barriers rather than the reactant populations. For precipitation the controlling quantity is nucleation: classical nucleation theory makes the critical radius depend on interfacial energy over supersaturation, so the phase with the lowest interfacial energy against the solution can nucleate first even when it is not the most stable bulk phase — Ostwald's rule made quantitative. The important epistemic point for a computational lab: any engine that minimises G is structurally incapable of discovering this, and must be told. That is why our kinetic thresholds are data with provenance rather than solver internals, and why the lab reports the phases it is deliberately withholding.

provenance.source: Ostwald, Zeitschrift für physikalische Chemie, 1897, for the rule of stages; standard treatments of kinetic versus thermodynamic control; Curtin-Hammett per standard physical organic chemistry; classical nucleation theory per standard treatments. log_k values for Cu(OH)2 (8.674) and Tenorite (7.644) from minteq.v4.dat (USGS/MINTEQA2). Editorial judgement (Kerotakis): the 340 K threshold at which we let tenorite form is a stated stand-in for a rate we do not model — every source we have describes the blue-to-black conversion qualitatively, so the number is chosen to match the demonstration rather than measured
provenance.computed_by: kerotakis-phreeqc (phase suppression via species::forms_only_above_k; saturation indices read back from the PHREEQC report)

concepts.definition_de: Die Alkalimetalle bilden die erste Hauptgruppe des Periodensystems. Alle Alkalimetalle reagieren heftig mit Wasser und bilden sehr leicht einfach positiv geladene Kationen. Alle Alkalimetalle besitzen genau ein Valenzelektron.

Die Elemente der zweiten Hauptgruppe werden auch als Erdalkalimetalle bezeichnet. Sie begegnen uns im Alltag als Spurenelemente und in Form von Mineralien. In ihren chemischen Eigenschaften weisen sie viele Ähnlichkeiten mit den Alkalimetallen der ersten Hauptgruppe auf.

Die Borgruppe - oder dritte Hauptgruppe - des Periodensystems der Elemente enthält einige technisch wichtige Elemente: Bor wird zur Dotierung von Halbleitern benötigt, Aluminium ist ein technisch wichtiger Werkstoff. Gallium und Indium werden in der Halbleiterindustrie verwendet. Alle Elemente der dritten Hauptgruppe besitzen drei Valenzelektronen.

Kohlenstoff ist eines der vielseitigsten Elemente der Chemie. Dieser kann mit seinen vier Valenzelektronen vier Bindungen zu anderen Atomen eingehen. Aber auch die anderen Elemente dieser Hauptgruppe sind zum Teil von großer technischer Bedeutung, so bildet beispielsweise Silizium die Grundlage der Halbleiterindustrie.
Stickstoff ist eines der häufigsten Elemente der Erde. Hauptgruppe, die sich letztlich auf das Vorhandensein von fünf Valenzelektronen zurückführen lassen.

Die Chalkogene - oder Erze - bilden die sechste Hauptgruppe des Periodensystems. Sie kommen häufig in Erzen vor, zum Beispiel in Form von Sulfiden und Oxiden. Gleichzeitig hat insbesondere das Element Sauerstoff eine herausragende Bedeutung für das Leben auf der Erde.

Die Halogene bilden die siebte Hauptgruppe. Alle elementaren Halogene sind sehr reaktionsfreudig, weshalb sie in der Natur meist als einfach negativ geladene Ionen vorkommen. Alle Halogene haben wichtige biochemische Funktionen als Bestandteile wichtiger Salze.

Das Abitur steht häufig am Ende der schulischen Laufbahn im Fach Chemie. Die Vorbereitung auf diese Abschlussprüfung ist jedoch nicht immer einfach. Hilfreich ist es, sich gezielt alte Klausuren anzusehen, die in großer Zahl im Internet zu finden sind.

Bei einer Additionsreaktion lagern sich Atome oder Moleküle an Doppel- oder Dreifachbindungen an und bilden Einfachbindungen aus. Dadurch entsteht aus zwei Molekülen ein neues Molekül. Die Addition kann nach verschiedenen Mechanismen ablaufen. Am bekanntesten ist die elektrophile Addition an Doppel- und Dreifachbindungen - die typische Reaktion der Alkene und Alkine.

Akkumulatoren - oft kurz Akkus genannt - sind Batterien, die wieder aufgeladen werden können. Ein klassisches Beispiel ist die Starterbatterie im Auto, der Bleiakku. Für Elektroautos werden sie immer wichtiger. Denn auch aus dem Alltag sind sie nicht mehr wegzudenken: Elektromobilität, Smartphones und kabellose Geräte für Garten, Freizeit und Hobby sind ohne immer leistungsfähigere Akkus kaum denkbar.

concepts.label_de: Aldehyde und Ketone - Oxidationsprodukte von Alkoholen
concepts.definition_de: Aldehyde und Ketone sind Oxidationsprodukte primärer und sekundärer Alkohole. Charakteristisch für Aldehyde und Ketone ist die Carbonylgruppe, die aus einem doppelt an ein Kohlenstoffatom gebundenen Sauerstoffatom besteht. Aldehyde und Ketone haben ein breites technisches und industrielles Anwendungsspektrum, z. B. als Reinigungsmittel wie Aceton in Nagellack, als Duft- und Aromastoffe und als Ausgangsstoffe für vielfältige chemische Synthesen.

Alkohole werden im Alltag vielfältig eingesetzt. Ethanol oder alkoholische Getränke sind alltäglich, aber auch ein Suchtmittel. Gleichzeitig wird es als Treibstoff verwendet und ist Ausgangspunkt für vielfältige Synthesen.

Alkohole sind eine Gruppe organischer Verbindungen, bei denen an einem Kohlenstoffatom mindestens ein Wasserstoffatom durch eine OH-Gruppe (Hydroxylgruppe) ersetzt ist. Diese funktionelle Gruppe beeinflusst die Eigenschaften der Alkohole sehr stark.

Amine sind organische Verbindungen, die als Verwandte des Ammoniaks angesehen werden können, da ein bis drei der Wasserstoffatome des Ammoniaks durch Kohlenwasserstoffreste ersetzt sind. Es gibt eine Vielzahl verschiedener Amine, die sich unter anderem in ihrer Struktur (Ring- oder Kettenstruktur) und in der Anzahl der im Molekül vorhandenen Stickstoffatome unterscheiden. Aufgrund dieser Vielfalt ist auch die Bandbreite der Stoffeigenschaften von Aminen sehr groß.

Analytische Verfahren spielen sowohl in der praktischen Anwendung der Chemie als auch in der Forschung eine zentrale Rolle. Sie können einerseits durch qualitative Nachweisreaktionen helfen zu klären, welche Stoffe in einer bestimmten Probe vorhanden sind. Andererseits können Chemiker:innen durch quantitative analytische Verfahren wie die Massenspektrometrie, spektroskopische sowie chromatographische Verfahren Aussagen über die Konzentration eines Analyten in einer Probe machen.

Zu Beginn des Chemieunterrichts geht es in der Regel um die Klärung des Stoffbegriffs sowie um die Eigenschaften chemischer Reaktionen. Denn diese sind mit der Zerstörung von Ausgangsstoffen und der Bildung neuer Stoffe sowie mit einem Energieumsatz verbunden.  Der Anfangsunterricht versucht, diese Grundlagen zu vermitteln.

Aromaten sind eine Stoffklasse organischer Verbindungen, die mindestens ein Ringsystem mit alternierenden - konjugierten - Doppelbindungen enthalten. Der bekannteste und zugleich einer der einfachsten Vertreter dieser Stoffklasse ist das Benzol. Aromatische Verbindungen verhalten sich oft anders, als ihre Strukturformel auf den ersten Blick vermuten lässt: Sie zeigen eben nicht die für Moleküle mit Doppelbindungen typischen Reaktionen, da ihr Doppelbindungssystem durch Mesomerie stabilisiert ist.

Das einfachste Atommodell geht davon aus, dass jeder Stoff aus kleinsten Teilchen besteht, die wiederum aus kugelförmigen, nicht weiter teilbaren Bausteinen zusammengesetzt sind: Atome. Diese Atome werden bei chemischen Reaktionen umgruppiert und neu zusammengesetzt, sind aber unzerstörbar. Mit Hilfe dieses Atommodells lassen sich Phänomene wie die Erhaltung der Masse bei chemischen Reaktionen erklären.

In der Chemie werden viele verschiedene Atommodelle verwendet. Jedes dieser Modelle hat seine Vor- und Nachteile. Der Chemieunterricht folgt bei der Einführung der Atommodelle oft der historischen Entwicklung: vom Atommodell von Dalton über das Kern-Hülle-Modell von Rutherford und das Schalenmodell von Bohr bis hin zu quantenmechanisch begründeten Modellen wie dem Orbitalmodell und dem daraus abgeleiteten Kugelwolkenmodell. Wenn du Materialien zu einzelnen Atommodellen suchst, bist du hier richtig. Materialien zum Periodensystem der Elemente findest du hingegen in der Rubrik “Anorganische Chemie”.

Chemische Reaktionen können mit Hilfe von Reaktionsgleichungen genau beschrieben werden. Durch geeignete Abbildungen wird dies verständlicher. Das Aufstellen und Ausgleichen von Reaktionsgleichungen erfordert jedoch Übung. Übungsmöglichkeiten finden sich hier.

Der Auftrieb ist eine Folge der unterschiedlichen Dichte zweier Stoffe. Die Menge des verdrängten Stoffes entscheidet darüber, ob z.B. ein Heißluftballon aufsteigt oder ein U-Boot sinkt. Zu dieser Schnittstelle zwischen Chemie und Physik findest du hier vielfältige Materialien.

Es gibt zahlreiche Batterietypen, die im Alltag eingesetzt werden. Allen gemeinsam ist, dass in zwei voneinander getrennten, aber elektrisch verbundenen Halbzellen eine RedOx-Reaktion abläuft. Die einzelnen Batterietypen unterscheiden sich durch den genauen Aufbau der Halbzellen - und wie die elektrische Verbindung der beiden Halbzellen realisiert wird. Einfache Batterien kann man mit wenigen Materialien zu Hause selbst bauen, kommerzielle Batterien sind oft deutlich komplexer aufgebaut.

Wie alle Moleküle können auch Alkohole mit systematischen Namen bezeichnet werden. Die Benennung der Alkohole basiert auf der homologen Reihe der Alkane, wobei zusätzlich die Position der Hydroxygruppe(n) angegeben wird.

Die Benennung der Kohlenwasserstoffe beruht auf den festgelegten Namen der homologen Reihe der Alkane. Die Benennung, auch Nomenklatur genannt, ist für die gesamte organische Chemie von zentraler Bedeutung, da nur so sinnvoll von organischen Verbindungen gesprochen werden kann und Edukte, Produkte und Übergangszustände organisch-chemischer Reaktionen eindeutig benannt werden können.

Benzol ist die einfachste aromatische Verbindung, die aus einem Ring mit 6 Kohlenstoffatomen und abwechselnden Doppelbindungen besteht. Benzol reagiert mit anderen Chemikalien ganz anders, als man aufgrund seiner Struktur intuitiv erwarten würde.

Mit Hilfe der Dichte lassen sich Volumenangaben in Massenangaben umrechnen und umgekehrt. Solche Umrechnungen sind besonders wichtig, wenn Gase oder Flüssigkeiten an einer Reaktion beteiligt sind. Die Dichte kann aber auch als Stoffeigenschaft aufgefasst werden, die es z. B. in der Pharmazie ermöglicht, zu prüfen, ob sich in einem Behälter tatsächlich der Stoff befindet, der darin enthalten sein soll.

Die Bewertungskompetenz beschreibt die Fähigkeit, sowohl persönliche Entscheidungen auf der Grundlage naturwissenschaftlichen Fachwissens zu treffen als auch - im Sinne der innerfachlichen Bewertung - chemische Sachverhalte im Hinblick auf ihre fachliche Richtigkeit zu beurteilen.

Chemische Bindungen bestimmen die beobachtbaren Eigenschaften der Materie. Es besteht also ein enger Zusammenhang zwischen den beobachtbaren Eigenschaften der Materie und den chemischen Bindungen und Strukturen auf Teilchenebene. Dies gilt sowohl für intramolekulare Bindungen wie die kovalente Bindung und die Ionenbindung als auch für intermolekulare Bindungen wie die Van-der-Waals-Kräfte und die Dipol-Dipol-Wechselwirkung.

Atome können sich zu größeren Einheiten verbinden, z. B. zu ionischen und metallischen Festkörpern oder zu Molekülen. Aus der Art der Bindung lässt sich meist recht genau erklären, warum ein Stoff bestimmte Eigenschaften hat. Dabei lassen sich die Grundtypen der chemischen Bindung unterscheiden: die Atombindung, die Ionenbindung, die Metallbindung und die koordinative Bindung. Metallbindung und die koordinative Bindung oder Komplexbindung.

Verbrennungen sind Reaktionen mit Sauerstoff. Sie sind oft die ersten Reaktionen, die im Chemieunterricht näher betrachtet werden. Sie lassen sich gut beobachten und bieten die Möglichkeit, etwas Neues zu lernen.

Säuren sind Moleküle, die Protonen an andere Moleküle abgeben können. Insbesondere organische Säuren sind Moleküle, die neben einem Kohlenwasserstoffrest mindestens eine spezielle Gruppe, die Carboxylgruppe, enthalten. Von dieser Carboxylgruppe werden bei Säure-Base-Reaktionen Protonen abgespalten. Das Besondere an diesen sogenannten Carbonsäuren ist ihre vergleichsweise geringe Säurestärke: Die meisten Carbonsäuren sind eher schwache Säuren - und spielen in unserem Alltag in Lebensmitteln, in der chemischen Industrie und als pH-Puffer eine herausragende Rolle.
